articles.title: कोलकाताबाट २४ घण्टामै नेपालमा ढुवानी, व्यवसायी उत्साहित
articles.summary:
मोरङ । उद्घाटन भएको करिब ३ वर्षपछि विराटनगरस्थित एकीकृत जाँच चौकीसम्म कार्गो रेलको सेवा पुनः शुरु भएको छ । पारवहन सन्धीको प्रोटोकल संसोधन पछि विराटनगरको एकीकृत जाँच चौकीस्थित नेपालको कस्टम यार्डसम्म कार्गो रेल आएको हो ।

विराटनगर स्थित एकिकृत जाँच चौकीसम्म कार्गो रेलको सेवा पुनः शुरु भएको छ । तत्कालिन प्रधानमन्त्री पुष्पकमल दाहाल प्रचण्ड र भारतका प्रधानमन्त्री नरेन्द्र मोदीले २०८० साल जेठ १८ गते उद्घाटन गरेयता कार्गो रेल आउन सकेको थिएन ।

मोरङको नेमुवास्थित स्वस्तिक आयल इण्डष्ट्रिजले मगाएको तोरी बोकेका ४० वटा कन्टेनरसहितको कार्गो रेल नेपाल भंसार यार्डसम्म आएको हो । रेल आएपछि सुनसरी मोरङ औद्योगिक करिडोरका उद्योगी व्यवसायीहरु उत्साहित भएका छन् ।

कार्गो रेलबाट ढुवानी गर्दा ढुवानी लागत २५ देखि ३० प्रतिशत घट्ने, कोलकाता बन्दरगाहबाट विराटनगरसम्म २४ घण्टामा सामान आईपुग्ने र बाटोमा सामान चोरी हुने समस्या निराकरण हुने भएकाले अन्य क्षेत्रका उद्योगहरुसँग प्रतिस्पर्धा गर्न सहज हुने उद्योगी व्यवसायीहरुले बताएका छन् ।

भारत सरकार अन्र्तर्गतको कन्कोर अर्थात कन्टेनर कर्पोरेशन अफ इण्डिया लिमिटेडको कार्गाे रेलबाट सोमवार एनसिवाई अर्थात नेपाल कस्टम यार्ड सम्म मालवाहक रेल आएको हो ।

कन्कोरका प्रतिनिधि संजिव साहले हप्तामा दुई दिन कोलकाताबाट विराटनगरसम्म कार्गो रेल संचालन गर्ने र यसलाई आवश्यकता अनुसार बढाउदै लैजाने जानकारी दिए ।

पारवहन सन्धीको प्रोटोकल संसोधनपछि विराटनगरको एकीकृत जाँच चौकीस्थित नेपाल कस्टम यार्डसम्म कार्गो रेल आएको हो । कार्गो रेल संचालन पछि विराटनगर आएको कन्टेनर खाली फर्कने भएकाले यहाँबाट वस्तु निर्यातमा पनि सहजता आउने उद्योगी व्यवसायीहरुले बताएका छन् ।

articles.title: प्युजो मोटरसाइकल्स नेपालद्वारा ‘Soirée Francaise’ आयोजना: फ्रान्सेली संस्कृति र जीवनशैलीको अनुभव
articles.summary:
अग्नि ग्रुप अन्तर्गतको प्युजो मोटरसाइकल्स नेपालले ‘Soirée Française – A Night of French Elegance’ शीर्षकमा एक विशेष 'फ्रेन्च फाइन डाइनिङ' कार्यक्रम सम्पन्न गरेको छ। काठमाडौँस्थित ला टेरास (La Terrasse) मा आयोजना गरिएको उक्त कार्यक्रममा प्युजोका विशिष्ट ग्राहक, व्यावसायिक साझेदार तथा फ्रान्सेली संस्कृतिप्रति आत्मियता राख्ने अतिथिहरूको उपस्थिति रहेको थियो।

कार्यक्रमले फ्रान्सको समृद्ध सांस्कृतिक विरासत र त्यसको प्रेरणादायी भावनालाई सम्मान गर्दै आपसी सम्बन्धलाई अझ सुदृढ बनाउने उद्देश्य राखेको थियो।

विश्वकपमा फ्रान्सेली टोलीको भावनाबाट प्रेरित

सन् २०२६ को फिफा विश्वकपमा फ्रान्सेली टोलीले प्रदर्शन गरेको समर्पण, दृढता, उत्कृष्टता र एकताको भावनाबाट प्रेरित भई यो कार्यक्रम आयोजना गरिएको हो। खेलको नतिजाभन्दा माथि उठेर फ्रान्सेली खेल संस्कृतिको अदम्य भावना र त्यसको विरासतलाई सम्मान गर्नु कार्यक्रमको मुख्य पक्ष थियो। यी मूल्यहरू प्युजो ब्रान्डको दीर्घकालीन पहिचानसँग समेत मेल खाने भएकाले सोही भावनालाई कार्यक्रममा प्रतिबिम्बित गरिएको थियो।

नेटवर्किङ र प्रिमियम जीवनशैलीको अनुभव

कार्यक्रममा सहभागी अतिथिहरूले पेरिस-प्रेरित आकर्षक सजावट तथा आत्मीय वातावरणमा विविध परम्परागत फ्रेन्च परिकारको स्वाद लिँदै नेटवर्किङको अनुभव सँगालेका थिए। प्युजोको फ्रान्सेली सम्पदालाई झल्काउँदै आफ्ना ग्राहकहरूप्रति कृतज्ञता व्यक्त गर्न र नेपालमा प्युजो समुदायसँगको सम्बन्धलाई अझ मजबुत बनाउन यस अवसरले सहयोग पुर्‍याएको कम्पनीले जनाएको छ।

ग्राहक केन्द्रित प्रतिबद्धता

यस अवसरमा प्युजो मोटरसाइकल्स नेपालका प्रतिनिधिहरूले गुणस्तरीय गतिशीलता (मोबिलिटी) समाधानका साथै ग्राहकलाई अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय स्तरको जीवनशैली अनुभव प्रदान गर्ने र विश्वव्यापी रूपमा प्युजोले प्रतिनिधित्व गर्ने मूल्य एवम् परम्परालाई निरन्तर अघि बढाउने प्रतिबद्धता पुनः व्यक्त गरे।

कार्यक्रमको समापन फ्रान्सेली संस्कृति, मित्रता र उत्कृष्टताको साझा भावनाप्रति सम्मान व्यक्त गर्दै ‘टोस्ट’ (Toast) का साथ गरिएको थियो। सहभागीहरूले यस अविस्मरणीय अनुभवले प्युजो मोटरसाइकल्स नेपाल र ग्राहकहरूबीचको प्रिमियम सम्बन्धलाई अझ सुदृढ बनाएको विश्वास व्यक्त गरेका छन्

articles.title: राष्ट्रिय इन्जिनियर दिवस घोषणा गर्न इन्जिनियर्स एसोसियसनको माग
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपाल इन्जिनियर्स एसोसियसनका अध्यक्ष सुवासचन्द्र बरालले प्रत्येक वर्ष साउन ३ गते मनाइने इन्जिनियर दिवसलाई सरकारले औपचारिक रूपमा ‘राष्ट्रिय इन्जिनियर दिवस’ घोषणा गरी सरकारी क्यालेन्डरमा समावेश गर्न आग्रह गरेका छन्।

एसोसियसनको ६४औँ इन्जिनियर दिवस समारोहलाई सम्बोधन गर्दै अध्यक्ष बरालले पूर्वाधार र प्रविधि कुनै पनि राष्ट्रको आर्थिक विकास र समृद्धिको मेरुदण्ड भएको उल्लेख गर्दै इन्जिनियरिङ क्षेत्रलाई प्राथमिकतामा राखेर राज्यले दीर्घकालीन नीति अवलम्बन गर्नुपर्ने बताए।

उनका अनुसार नेपालमा दर्ता भएका करिब एक लाख इन्जिनियरमध्ये करिब ६० प्रतिशत युवा छन्। तर पर्याप्त रोजगारी र अवसरको अभावका कारण ठूलो संख्यामा दक्ष जनशक्ति विदेश पलायन भइरहेको भन्दै उनले यसलाई रोक्न तत्काल प्रभावकारी नीति आवश्यक रहेको बताए।

‘युवा इन्जिनियरहरूको सीप, ज्ञान र दक्षताको उचित उपयोग गर्न राज्य, उद्योग र इन्जिनियरिङ समुदायबीच बलियो सहकार्य आवश्यक छ,’ उनले भने।

बरालले यस वर्षको इन्जिनियर दिवस 'Young Mind and Engineering: Shaping Better Nepal' भन्ने मूल नारासहित मनाइएको जानकारी दिँदै विकास निर्माणमा संलग्न प्राविधिकहरूले कार्यस्थलमा असुरक्षा, प्रशासनिक झन्झट र अनावश्यक दबाब झेल्नुपरेको गुनासो गरे। यस्तो अवस्थाले विकास आयोजनाको गति नै प्रभावित भएको उनको भनाइ थियो।

उनले प्राविधिकहरूको क्षमताको अधिकतम उपयोग गर्न पुरस्कार र दण्डको स्पष्ट प्रणाली लागू गर्नुपर्ने आवश्यकता औँल्याए। ऊर्जा, जलस्रोत, कृषि, पर्यटन, सूचना प्रविधि, उद्योग तथा मानव संसाधनलगायत सबै क्षेत्रमा इन्जिनियरहरूको भूमिका निर्णायक रहेको उल्लेख गर्दै बदलिँदो प्रविधिअनुसार सीप विकासमा लगानी बढाउनुपर्नेमा जोड दिए।

सरकारसमक्ष एसोसियसनले इन्जिनियरिङ क्षेत्रसँग सम्बन्धित विभिन्न नीतिगत माग पनि अघि सारेको छ।

अध्यक्ष बरालले विकास निर्माणमा खटिने इन्जिनियरका लागि सुरक्षित कार्य वातावरणको कानुनी प्रत्याभूति, रणनीतिक सरकारी निकायको नेतृत्व तहमा प्राविधिक पृष्ठभूमिका इन्जिनियरहरूको प्रतिनिधित्व, छुट्टै इन्जिनियरिङ सेवा आयोग गठन तथा नेपाल इन्जिनियरिङ प्रशिक्षण तथा अनुसन्धान प्रतिष्ठान स्थापना प्रक्रिया तत्काल अघि बढाउन आग्रह गरे।

त्यसैगरी, युवा इन्जिनियरका लागि पर्याप्त रोजगारी सिर्जना, विकास आयोजनाको सुपरभिजन इन्जिनियरबाटै गराउने व्यवस्था, निजी तथा गैरसरकारी क्षेत्रमा कार्यरत इन्जिनियरहरूको न्यूनतम मासिक पारिश्रमिक ३७ हजार १३५ कार्यान्वयन तथा प्राविधिक त्रुटिलाई स्वतः भ्रष्टाचारको कसुर अन्तर्गत नराख्ने कानुनी व्यवस्था गर्न पनि उनले सरकारसँग माग गरे।

अध्यक्ष बरालले नेपाल इन्जिनियर्स एसोसियसन इन्जिनियरहरूको पेशागत हकहितको संरक्षण, नवप्रवर्तनको प्रवर्द्धन र राज्यसँग इन्जिनियरिङ समुदायलाई जोड्ने साझा संस्थाका रूपमा निरन्तर सक्रिय रहने प्रतिबद्धता व्यक्त गर्दै सम्पूर्ण इन्जिनियर तथा आर्किटेक्टलाई पेशागत नैतिकता र इमान्दारितालाई सर्वोच्च प्राथमिकतामा राखेर समृद्ध नेपाल निर्माणमा योगदान दिन आह्वान गरे।

articles.title: जेनजी आन्दोलन प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयनमा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय दबाब
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । गत वर्षको भदौ २३ र २४ गते देशमा भएको जेनजी विद्रोह र त्यसक्रममा भएका गम्भीर मानवअधिकार उल्लंघनका घटनासम्बन्धी राष्ट्रिय मानवअधिकार आयोगको प्रतिवेदन संयुक्त राष्ट्रसंघ पुगेको छ ।

नेपालभित्र प्रतिवेदन सार्वजनिक गर्न चौतर्फी माग भइरहेका बेला आयोगले करिब १० हजार पृष्ठ लामो उक्त प्रतिवेदन जेनेभास्थित मानवअधिकार उच्चायुक्तको कार्यालयमा पेश गरेको छ।

तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री केपी शर्मा ओली र गृहमन्त्री रमेश लेखकसहित उच्च अधिकारीहरूमाथि फौजदारी अनुसन्धानको सिफारिस गरिएको यो प्रतिवेदन अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय मञ्चमा पुगेसँगै अब सरकारमाथि कूटनीतिक र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय दबाब बढ्ने देखिएको छ ।

गएको भदौ २३–२४ गतेको जेनजी विद्रोहसम्बन्धी राष्ट्रिय मानवअधिकार आयोगको प्रतिवेदन संयुक्त राष्ट्रसंघीय मानव अधिकार उच्चायुक्तको कार्यालय ओएचसीएचआर जेनेभामा पेश भएको छ ।

यो प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयनका लागि अब सरकारलाई थप दबाब पर्नेछ । जुन १५ देखि जुलाइ ७ सम्म जेनेभामा चलेको ह्युमन राइट काउन्सिलको २४औँ बैठक र ६२ औँ सत्रमा राष्ट्रिय मानवअधिकार आयोगका सदस्य मिहिर ठाकुरले नेपालमा भएको जेनजी विद्रोहको मानवअधिकार अवस्थाका विस्तृत विवरणसहितको प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयनका लागि सरकारलाई बुझाएको जानकारी दिँदै सरकारले प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वय गर्नैपर्ने जानकारी गराएका थिए ।

उच्चायुक्तको कार्यालयले राष्ट्रिय मानवअधिकार आयोगले पेश गरेको प्रतिवेदनलाई नोटमा राखेको छ । सरकारलाई मानवअधिकार आयोगको प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयनका लागि अरु दबाब पर्नेछ । जेनेभा बैठकमा भाग लिन आयोगका सदस्य ठाकुरसँगै आयोगकी उपसचिव माया शर्मा पनि पुगेकी थिइन ।

सरकारमाथि अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय दबाब बढाउने रणनीति

आयोगभित्रैका केही अधिकारीहरूका अनुसार सरकारले प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयन नगर्ने आशंका बढेपछि आयोगले प्रतिवेदन अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय मञ्चमा पठाएको हो ।

नेपालमै प्रतिवेदन पूर्णरूपमा सार्वजनिक गर्न आग्रह मानव अधिकार आयोगले आग्रह गरे पनि त्यो सम्भव नभएको बताउने गरेकाले पनि अब जेनेभाबाटै थप प्रक्रिया अगाडि बढ्न सक्ने अवस्था बनेको छ ।

प्रतिवेदनमा को–कोमाथि अनुसन्धान सिफारिस ?

जेनजी आन्दोलनमा भएको दमन, गोली प्रहार, सार्वजनिक सम्पत्तिमा आगजनी तथा विध्वंसका घटनाबारे आयेगको प्रतिवेदन करिब १० हजार पृष्ठको छ । तर आयोगले प्रतिवेदनको केही अंश मात्रै सार्वजनिक गरेको थियो ।

उक्त प्रतिवेदनमा तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री केपी शर्मा ओली, तत्कालीन गृहमन्त्री रमेश लेखक, तत्कालीन सञ्चारमन्त्री पृथ्वी सुब्बा गुरुङ, तत्कालीन प्रहरी महानिरीक्षक चन्द्रकुवेर खापुङ लगायतमाथि फौजदारी अनुसन्धान अघि बढाउन सिफारिस गरिएको छ ।

यसैगरी आन्दोलनका क्रममा भएको विध्वंसमा कलाकार, पत्रकार, इन्फ्लुएन्सर तथा हाल संसद् र सरकारमा रहेका केही व्यक्तिहरूमाथि पनि थप अनुसन्धान गर्न आयोगले सिफारिस गरेको छ ।

आन्दोलनका घटनाबारे आयोगको निष्कर्ष

पूर्ण प्रतिवेदनमा भदौ २३ देखि २६ सम्मका घटना समेटिएका छन् । कसले कोसँग संवाद ग¥यो ?के–के कुरा भयो ? सार्वजनिक सम्पत्तिमा आगो लगाउनेसम्ममा कसको योजना थियो भन्ने समेटिएका छन् ।

भीड कसरी उग्र बन्यो, सार्वजनिक सम्पत्तिमा आगजनी गर्ने योजना कसरी बनेको थियो भन्ने विवरण पनि प्रतिवेदनमा समावेश छ । आयोगले अनुसन्धानका लागि आवश्यक केही प्रमाण, विशेषगरी गोलीका अवशेष बुलेट संकलन गर्न नसकिएको स्वीकार गरेको छ ।

ओली–लेखकले नै मागेका छन्, प्रतिवेदनको प्रतिलिपि

आयोगको पूर्ण प्रतिवेदन सार्वजनिक गर्न माग भइरहँदा फौजदारी अनुसन्धान अघि बढाउन सिफारिस गरिएका पूर्व प्रधानमन्त्री एवम् एमाले अध्यक्ष ओली, पूर्व गृहमन्त्री एवम् कांग्रेस नेता रमेश लेखक, पूर्व सञ्चार मन्त्री पृथ्वी सुब्बा गुरुङले प्रतिवेदनमाथि प्रश्न उठाउँदै आयोगसमक्ष निवेदन दर्ता गराएका छन् ।

प्रतिवेदनको केही अंश झिकिएको र केही अंश थपिएको आशंकापछि उनीहरुले प्रतिवेदन माग गरेका हुन् । ओलीको तर्फबाट छानबिन तथा अनुसन्धान प्रतिवेदन माग गर्दै एमाले नेता महेश बर्तौलाले असार १२ गते आयोगमा निवेदन दर्ता गराएका थिए ।

ओलीले आयोगको बैठकको निर्णय नम्बर १७७ को प्रमाणित प्रतिलिपि, लिली थापा नेतृत्वको समितिले आयोगमा पेश गरेको प्रतिवेदनको प्रतिलिपि, प्रतिवेदनमा थपघट गरिएको अंश र थपघट गर्नुको कारणसमेत माग गरेका छन् ।

यस्तै, रास्वपा सभापति रवि लामिछानेलाई कारागारबाट बाहिर निकाल्न गएको आरोप लागेका सांसद दीपक बोहोराले पनि आयोगमा निवेदन दिएका थिए । आयोगले भनेको समयमा आफू अस्पतालमा रहेको उनको दलिल छ ।

उच्चायुक्तको कार्यालयमा प्रतिवेदन पेश भएपछि के हुन्छ ?

संयुक्त राष्ट्रसंघको मानवअधिकार उच्चायुक्तको कार्यालयले अब चार चरणमा प्रक्रिया अघि बढाउँछ ।

पहिलो चरण : अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय अभिलेखः–

प्रतिवेदन संयुक्त राष्ट्रसंघको आधिकारिक अभिलेखमा दर्ता हुन्छ । यसले नेपालमा मानव अधिकार उल्लंघन भएको दाबी अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय निगरानीमा प्रवेश गर्छ ।

दोस्रो चरण : प्रश्न र स्पष्टीकरणः–

मानव अधिकार परिषद्का सदस्य राष्ट्रहरूले नेपाल सरकारसँग स्पष्टीकरण माग्न सक्छन् ।

तेस्रो चरण : सिफारिसः–

उच्चायुक्तको कार्यालय वा विशेष प्रतिवेदकहरूले नेपाललाई अनुसन्धान, पीडितलाई क्षतिपूर्ति वा जिम्मेवार व्यक्तिमाथि कारबाही गर्न सिफारिस गर्न सक्छन् ।

चौथो चरण : निगरानीः–

नेपालले ती सिफारिस कार्यान्वयन ग¥यो कि गरेन भनेर आगामी सत्रहरूमा पुनःसमीक्षा हुन्छ ।

जेनजी प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयनमा दबाब

जेनजी आन्दोलनको प्रतिवेदन अब नेपालको आन्तरिक राजनीतिक विवाद मात्र रहेन, अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय मानव अधिकार बहसको विषय बनेको छ । मानव अधिकार परिषद्को ६२औँ सत्रमा यसबारे औपचारिक जानकारी प्रस्तुत भइसकेकाले नेपाल सरकारले प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयन नगरेमा आगामी सत्रहरूमा थप प्रश्न उठ्न सक्छन् ।

यद्यपी प्रतिवेदन कार्यान्वयन नगरेकै कारण कुनै देशलाई तुरुन्त प्रतिबन्ध भने लाग्दैन ।तर अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय आलोचना बढ्छ । मानव अधिकार सम्बन्धी वार्षिक प्रतिवेदनमा नकारात्मक उल्लेख हुन्छ । यसको असरले वैदेशिक सहायता र विकास साझेदारहरूको दबाब बढ्न सक्छ ।

त्यस्तै, विशेष प्रतिवेदक वा अनुसन्धान टोली पठाउने सम्भावना पनि रहन्छ। नेपालमा विगतमा द्वन्द्वकालीन मानव अधिकार उल्लंघनका विषयमा संयुक्त राष्ट्रसंघले पटक–पटक चासो व्यक्त गरेको छ ।

यस्ता घटनामा कुन कुन देशलाई प्रतिबन्ध लागेको छ ?

मानव अधिकार उल्लंघनका आधारमा विभिन्न देशहरूमा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय प्रतिबन्ध लगाइएको उदाहरणहरु छन् । म्यानमारमा सैन्य दमन र मानव अधिकार उल्लंघनको घटनामा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय प्रतिबन्ध लगाइएको छ भने इरानमा प्रदर्शनकारीमाथि दमन गरेको भन्दै मानवअधिकार उल्लंघन भएको निश्कर्षमा प्रतिबन्ध लगाइएको छ।

त्यस्तै मानवअधिकार उल्लंघनका घटना छानबिन गरेर कारवाही नगरेका कारण बेलारुस, गृहयुद्ध र मानवअधिकार उल्लंघनका कारण सिरिया लगायतका देश प्रतिबन्धमा परेका छन् ।

articles.title: झापाका ४२ परिवार तनावमा, अन्तिम किस्ता रोकिएपछि छटपटि
articles.summary:
झापा । झापाको मेचीनगरस्थित दिपज्योती टोलका ४२ परिवार दुई दशकअघि किस्ताबन्दीमा खरिद गरेको जग्गाको लालपूर्जा नपाउँदा समस्यामा परेका छन् । मेचीनगर २ र ३ को सिमानास्थित जग्गा हालसम्म नामसारी हुन नसक्दा पीडित परिवारको समस्या झन् जटिल बन्दै गएको छ ।

झापाको मेचीनगर ३ स्थित बजगाई टि–स्टेट प्रालिको नाममा रहेको चिया बगान नभएको खाली जग्गा वि.स २०६३÷०६४ सालमा शुभ चिया प्रालिले बैना गरि घरघडेरीका लागि स्थानीयलाई किस्ताबन्दी एकदेखि पाँच कठ्ठासम्म बिक्री प्रक्रिया अगाडी बढायो ।

सुकुम्बासी तथा न्यून आय भएका परिवारलाई लक्षित गरी बिक्री गरिएको उक्त जग्गाको अधिकांश किस्ता तिरे पनि अन्तिम किस्ता लिएपछि लालपूर्जा उपलब्ध गराउने सहमति कार्यान्वयन नभएको पीडितहरूको भनाइ छ ।

अन्तिम किस्ता पनि तिर्न तयार भएका उनीहरुको संस्थाले रकम नै लिएन । अहिले उनीहरुको न पैसा फिर्ता भएको छ, न लालपूर्जा नै पाएका छन् ।

त्यस्तै पीडित स्थानीयका अनुसार जग्गा बजगाई टि–स्टेट प्रालिको नाममा रहे पनि तत्कालीन शुभ चिया प्रालिका अध्यक्ष हेमराज भारतीले कारोबार अगाडी बढाएका थिए । तर उनले पैसा लिएपछि त्यसलाई कार्यान्वयन गर्न आलटाल गरेको दुखेसो पीडित पोख्छन् । उनीहरुले जग्गा समस्या तत्काल समाधानका लागि सम्बन्धित निकायसँग माग गरेका छन्।

यता शुभ चिया प्रालिका वर्तमान अध्यक्ष रमेश दाहालले विगतमा कारोबार संस्थागत प्रक्रियाअनुसार नभएकाले समस्या उत्पन्न भएको बताउँछन् । समस्या समाधानका लागि सम्बन्धित सरोकारवाला निकायसँग आवश्यक गृहकार्य भइरहेको र पीडितलाई न्याय दिलाउने प्रयास जारी रहेको उनको भनाइ छ ।

सुकुम्बासी तथा न्यून आय भएका परिवारले साहुसंग ऋण गरेर किस्ता वापतको रकम समेत दिइ सकेको अवस्थामा अन्तिम किस्ता नलिई जग्गाको स्वामित्व समेत प्रदान नगर्दा ४२ परिवार समस्यामा परेका छन् । तसर्थ उनीहरुलाई सम्बन्धित सरोकारवाला निकायले यथाशिघ्र समस्या समाधान गर्नुपर्ने आवश्यक देखिन्छ ।

articles.title: नेपाल लाइफको ऐतिहासिक कीर्तिमान, १३ अर्बभन्दा बढी प्रथम बीमा आर्जन
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । नेपालको सर्वाधिक विश्वासिलो जीवन बीमा कम्पनीका रूपमा स्थापित नेपाल लाइफ इन्स्योरेन्सले आफ्नो २५ वर्षको गौरवमय यात्रा (सिल्भर जुबिली) का अवसरमा रु. १३ अर्बभन्दा बढी प्रथम बीमा शुल्क (FPI) आर्जन गर्दै जीवन बीमा इतिहासमा नयाँ ऐतिहासिक कीर्तिमान कायम गरेको छ।

गत आर्थिक वर्षमा रु. १० अर्ब प्रथम बीमा शुल्क आर्जन गरेको कम्पनीले यस वर्ष उक्त उपलब्धिलाई अझ उचाइमा पुर्‍याउँदै बीमा उद्योगमा नयाँ मानक स्थापित गरेको हो।

यस ऐतिहासिक सफलताका अवसरमा कम्पनीका प्रमुख कार्यकारी अधिकृत प्रवीण रमण पराजुलीले सम्पूर्ण बीमित, अभिकर्ता, कर्मचारी, शेयरधनी तथा सरोकारवालाहरू प्रति आभार व्यक्त गर्दै आगामी दिनमा अझ थप प्रविधिमैत्री सेवा, नवीन बीमा योजना र उत्कृष्ट सेवा प्रदान गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता व्यक्त गरे ।

articles.title: सिद्धार्थ बैंकद्वारा ‘सिद्धार्थ गोल्ड लोन’ सुविधा सञ्चालनमा
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । सिद्धार्थ बैंक लिमिटेडले ग्राहकहरुको तत्कालको वित्तीय आवश्यकतालाई सहज र सर्वसुलभ बनाउने उद्देश्यका साथ नयाँ कर्जा योजना ‘सिद्धार्थ गोल्ड लोन’ सार्वजनिक गरेको छ।

यस योजना अन्तर्गत ग्राहकहरुले आफ्नो सुन तथा सुनका गरगहनाहरु धितो राखी बैंकबाट अधिकतम रु. ५० लाखसम्मको कर्जा रकम प्राप्त गर्न सक्नेछन्, जसमा धितो सुनको मूल्यांकनका आधारमा बढीमा ७५ प्रतिशतसम्म कर्जा प्रवाह गरिनेछ।

ग्राहकहरूले आफ्नो व्यक्तिगत तथा व्यावसायिक आवश्यकता सहज रूपमा पूरा गर्न सकुन् भन्ने उद्देश्यले सञ्चालनमा ल्याइएको यो सुरक्षित र भरपर्दो सुविधा हालका लागि बैंकको काठमाडौंस्थित न्यूरोड गेट शाखाबाट उपलब्ध छ, र यस सम्बन्धी थप जानकारीका लागि बैंकको २४ सै घण्टा सञ्चालनमा रहने ग्राहक सेवा केन्द्र ‘सिद्धार्थ केयर’ मा सम्पर्क गर्न सकिनेछ।

articles.title: कतारमा नेपाली समुदायद्वारा स्वर्गीय फादर अमिरप्रति श्रद्धाञ्जली
articles.summary:
कतार । गैरआवासीय नेपाली संघ (एनआरएनए) राष्ट्रिय समन्वय परिषद् (एनसीसी) कतारले स्वर्गीय हिज हाइनेस फादर अमिर शेख हमद बिन खलिफा अल थानीप्रति श्रद्धाञ्जली अर्पण गर्न शोकसभा आयोजना गरेको छ।

कार्यक्रममा उनको दूरदर्शी नेतृत्व तथा कतारको समृद्धि, विकास र विश्वमञ्चमा स्थापित गराउन पुर्‍याएको अतुलनीय योगदानको उच्च सम्मान गरिएको थियो।

कार्यक्रममा कतारस्थित नेपाली राजदूतावासका कूटनीतिज्ञ प्रेमप्रसाद पोखरेल प्रमुख अतिथिका रूपमा सहभागी भएका थिए। साथै कतारमा क्रियाशील विभिन्न नेपाली सामाजिक तथा कल्याणकारी संस्थाका प्रतिनिधिहरूको उल्लेखनीय उपस्थिति रहेको थियो। शोकको यस घडीमा नेपाली समुदायले एकता र ऐक्यबद्धता प्रदर्शन गरेको आयोजकले जनाएको छ।

कार्यक्रमको सुरुआत पवित्र कुरआनको तिलावतबाट भएको थियो भने मौलाना गुलाम नबी रजबीले स्वर्गीय फादर अमिरको आत्माको चिरशान्तिको कामना गर्दै कतार राज्यको शान्ति, स्थायित्व र समृद्धिका लागि विशेष दुआ गरेका थिए।

एनआरएनए एनसीसी कतारका अध्यक्ष कृष्ण पन्थीले स्वागत मन्तव्य दिँदै स्वर्गीय फादर अमिरको निधनप्रति गहिरो दुःख व्यक्त गरे।

उनले कतारका अमिर, राजपरिवार, सरकार तथा सम्पूर्ण कतारी जनताप्रति समवेदना व्यक्त गर्दै स्वर्गीय फादर अमिरको दूरदर्शी नेतृत्व, राष्ट्र निर्माणमा खेलेको ऐतिहासिक भूमिका र उनले छोडेको प्रेरणादायी विरासतको प्रशंसा गरे। पन्थीले कतारलाई विश्वकै सम्मानित र समृद्ध राष्ट्रका रूपमा स्थापित गर्न फादर अमिरको योगदान अविस्मरणीय रहेको बताए।

कार्यक्रमका प्रमुख वक्ता प्राध्यापक मोहम्मद रमजान अली मियाँले नेपाल–कतारबीचको लामो समयदेखिको मित्रवत सम्बन्ध र बढ्दो सहकार्यबारे चर्चा गरे। उनले स्वर्गीय फादर अमिरको नेतृत्वमा कतारले आर्थिक विविधीकरण, शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, पूर्वाधार विकास तथा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय कूटनीतिमा उल्लेखनीय प्रगति हासिल गरेको बताए। साथै कतारले हजारौँ नेपालीलाई रोजगारी तथा अवसर उपलब्ध गराउँदै आएको उल्लेख गर्दै त्यसप्रति आभार व्यक्त गरे।

कतारस्थित नेपाली दूतावासका तर्फबाट बोल्दै कूटनीतिज्ञ प्रेमप्रसाद पोखरेलले स्वर्गीय फादर अमिरप्रति श्रद्धाञ्जली अर्पण गर्दै उनको योगदानको उच्च प्रशंसा गरे।

उनले नेपाल–कतारबीचको मैत्रीपूर्ण सम्बन्ध निरन्तर सुदृढ हुँदै आएको उल्लेख गर्दै आगामी दिनमा दुई देशबीचको सहयोग र मित्रतालाई अझ मजबुत बनाउने प्रतिबद्धता व्यक्त गरे।

कार्यक्रममा सहभागी विभिन्न नेपाली संघ–संस्थाका प्रतिनिधिहरूले पनि शोक मन्तव्य व्यक्त गर्दै कतारले नेपाली समुदायलाई प्रदान गरेको अवसरप्रति आभार प्रकट गरे। साथै कठिन घडीमा कतारका नेतृत्व र जनताप्रति ऐक्यबद्धता तथा सम्मान व्यक्त गरे।

श्रद्धाञ्जली सभा अन्त्यमा स्वर्गीय हिज हाइनेस शेख हमद बिन खलिफा अल थानीको सम्मानमा सामूहिक प्रार्थना तथा एक मिनेट मौनधारण गरिएको थियो। कार्यक्रममा वक्ताहरूले उनको दूरदर्शी नेतृत्व र योगदानले आगामी पुस्तालाई पनि प्रेरणा दिइरहने विश्वास व्यक्त गरेका थिए।

articles.title: मिटर ब्याज पीडितलाई मनाउन सुधनको कसरत, बल्ल माने पीडित
articles.summary:
बारा । बाराको निजगढ नगरपालिका–८ स्थित निजगढ नगर उद्योग वाणिज्य संघको सभाहलमा तीन दिनदेखि जारी सरकार र मिटरब्याजविरुद्ध किसान–मजदुर आन्दोलनको निर्णायक वार्ता अब राजधानी काठमाडौंमा हुने भएको छ । मिटरब्याज पीडित सरकारसँग वार्ता गर्न जहाजबाट काठमाडौं आएका छन् ।

जनकपुरबाट काठमाडौंतर्फ पैदल न्याय मार्चमा रहेका मिटरब्याजविरुद्ध किसान–मजदुर आन्दोलन, नेपालका प्रतिनिधिहरूसँग गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङले बुधबार करिब पाँच घण्टा लामो छलफल गरेका थिए । छलफलका क्रममा आन्दोलनकारीहरूले उठाएका छ बुँदे मागबारे विस्तृत रूपमा कुराकानी भएको थियो ।

आन्दोलन पक्षका अनुसार सरकारले उनीहरूले अघि सारेका सम्पूर्ण माग कार्यान्वयन गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता जनाएको छ । बुधबार राति निष्कर्षविहीन बनेको वार्तापछि नेपाल सरकारका गृहमन्त्री सुदन गुरुङले आन्दोलनकारीलाई वार्ता टोली गठन गरी सिंहदरबारस्थित गृह मन्त्रालयमा आउन आग्रह गरेका थिए ।

वार्ताका क्रममा गृहमन्त्री गुरुङले सहमतिपत्रमा रहेका केही शब्द तथा भाषागत विषयमा संशोधन गर्न आवश्यक रहेको बताएका थिए । कानुनी तथा प्राविधिक पक्षसमेत मिलाउनुपर्ने भएकाले तत्काल हस्ताक्षर गर्नु उपयुक्त नहुने उनको भनाइ थियो ।

त्यसपछि गृहमन्त्रीको पटक–पटकको आग्रह र आन्दोलनकारी पक्षको आन्तरिक छलफलपछि मिटरब्याजविरुद्ध किसान–मजदुर आन्दोलन, नेपालले पाँच सदस्यीय वार्ता टोली गठन गरी बिहीबार काठमाडौं प्रस्थान गरेको हो । अन्य आन्दोलनकारी भने वार्ताको नतिजा नआएसम्म बाराको निजगढमै रहने जनाइएको छ ।

काठमाडौं प्रस्थान आएको पाँच सदस्यीय वार्ता टोलीको संयोजकमा केन्द्रीय अध्यक्ष अवधेश कुश्वाहा रहेका छन् । टोलीमा केन्द्रीय महासचिव मनोज कुमार पासवान, केन्द्रीय प्रवक्ता रिजन राना मगर, केन्द्रीय हेडक्वाटर सदस्य लक्ष्मी घिमिरे तथा केन्द्रीय हेडक्वाटर सदस्य किरण परियार सदस्य रहेका छन् । वार्ता टोलीको रोहबरमा संयुक्त जनअधिकार मोर्चाका केन्द्रीय अध्यक्ष निर्ग नवीन लगायतका प्रतिनिधिहरू पनि काठमाडौं आएका छन् ।

आन्दोलनका केन्द्रीय अध्यक्ष अवधेश कुश्वाहाले सरकारले माग पूरा गर्न सकारात्मक प्रतिबद्धता जनाएको भए पनि त्यसलाई कानुनी रूपमा स्पष्ट र लिखित रूपमा सुनिश्चित गर्नुपर्ने बताए ।

उनले आन्दोलनकारीको उद्देश्य सहमतिपत्रमा हस्ताक्षर मात्र नभई त्यसको प्रभावकारी कार्यान्वयन सुनिश्चित गर्नु रहेको उल््लेख गर्दै वार्ता सकारात्मक निष्कर्षमा पुग्ने विश्वास व्यक्त गरेका छन् ।

articles.title: कांग्रेस नेता अभिषेक गिरीको अपराध साम्राज्य !
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । ‘हिजो गल्ती भयो, अब समाजसेवामा लाग्छु’ भनी करिब तीन वर्षअघि कारागारबाट छुट्दा अभिषेक गिरीले दिएको सन्देशले धेरैलाई उनी बदलिएको विश्वास दिलाएको थियो । तर, समाजसेवाको आवरणमा पुरानै आपराधिक सञ्जाल सञ्चालन गरेको आरोपमा अहिले उनी फेरि प्रहरी नियन्त्रणमा छन् । मोरङ प्रहरी र केन्द्रीय अनुसन्धान ब्युरो (सीआईबी) दुवैले उनीविरुद्ध ठगी र आपराधिक विश्वासघातसम्बन्धी उजुरीमाथि अनुसन्धान गरिरहेका छन् ।

२०७९ चैत ५ गते नौ वर्ष जेल सजाय भुक्तान गरेर कारागारबाट निस्कँदा अभिषेक गिरी साधु भएको आभाष दिलाएका थिए । विगतका गल्ती नदोहो¥याउने प्रतिवद्धता जनाउँदै उनले समाजसेवामा समर्पित हुने घोषणा गरेका थिए ।

त्यसपछि उनले ‘गिरी फाउन्डेसन’ स्थापना गरे, सामाजिक कार्यक्रममा सक्रिय देखिए र आर्थिक रूपमा विपन्नलाई सहयोग गर्न थाले । तर, प्रहरी अनुसन्धानले अभिषेक समाजसेवाको आडमा आपराधिक क्रियाकलापमा संलग्न रहेको भन्दै गम्भीर प्रश्न उठाएको छ ।

गिरीमाथि लागेको आरोप के हो ?

अहिले सीआईबीले अनुसन्धानका लागि मोरङबाट काठमाडौं ल्याएका गिरीलाई यसअघि जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय मोरङले पक्राउ गरेको थियो । उनी पक्राउ परेको विषय पनि निकै रोचक छ । कारागार बाहिरका मान्छेको कारागारभित्र कुनै पहुँच हुँदैन ।

कुनै कैदीबन्दीलाई भेट्न जानु प¥यो भने पनि भेटघाटको कारण खुलाउँदै प्रशासनको अनुमति लिएर सुरक्षा जाँच पार गर्नुपर्ने हुन्छ । अझ कारागारभित्रको प्रशासनको बाहिर कुनै साइनो नै हुँदैन । यति सुरक्षित रहने कारागारको शासन भने गिरीले बाहिरै बसेर चलाउँथे ।

कैदीबन्दीको रासन भत्तामा समेत कब्जा जमाएर असुल्ने गरेको भन्दै गिरीविरुद्ध कैदीबन्दीले नै आवाज उठाएका थिए ।

कैदीबन्दीले बनाएको मुढा र गलैँचाको पैसा गिरीले बुझ्ने गरेको आरोप छ । असार १२ गते कैदीबन्दीलाई बाँडेको १३ लाख ४० हजार रुपैयाँ असुल गरेको आरोप पनि गिरीमाथि छ ।

कारागारभित्रको खाद्यान्न र तरकारी आपूर्तिमा समेत उनको सिन्डिकेट चल्ने गरेको कैदीबन्दीको गुनासो थियो । प्रहरीका अनुसार, गिरीमाथि अहिले दुई फरक प्रकृतिका आरोपमा अनुसन्धान भइरहेको छ ।

मोरङमा कारागारभित्र हुने आर्थिक गतिविधिमा बाहिरबाट प्रभाव पार्दै कैदीबन्दीको रासन भत्ता, उनीहरूले उत्पादन गरेका सामग्रीको रकम तथा आपूर्ति व्यवस्थामा अवैध हस्तक्षेप गरेको आरोपका आधारमा असार १३ गते मोरङ प्रहरीले उनलाई पक्राउ गरेको हो । उनको घरमा गरिएको खानतलासीका क्रममा नगद गन्ने मेसिनसमेत फेला परेको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ ।

उच्च अदालत विराटनगरको आदेशपछि उनी मोरङबाट छुटे पनि त्यही दिन सीआईबीले पुनः नियन्त्रणमा लियो । यसपटक भने निर्माण व्यवसायी सुवास श्रेष्ठको उजुरीका आधारमा अनुसन्धान अघि बढाइएको छ ।

पहुँचका आधारमा ठेक्का दिलाइदिने आश्वासन दिएर ठगी गरेको, निर्माण उपकरण नियन्त्रणमा लिएको तथा जबर्जस्ती सम्पत्ति हस्तान्तरण गराएको आरोपमा आपराधिक विश्वासघात र ठगीसम्बन्धी अनुसन्धान भइरहेको सीआईबीको भनाइ छ । प्रहरीले घटनासँग सम्बन्धित प्रमाण संकलन र बयान लिने काम जारी रहेको जनाएको छ ।

अभिषेक गिरीको आपराधिक पृष्ठभूमि

अभिषेक गिरीको आपराधिक पृष्ठभूमि भने लामो छ । प्रहरीको अभिलेखअनुसार उनी पहिलो पटक २०५८ सालमा पक्राउ परेका थिए । त्यसयता कुटपिट, सार्वजनिक अपराध, डाँका चोरी, ज्यान मार्ने उद्योग र अन्ततः अपहरण तथा शरीर बन्धकजस्ता विभिन्न मुद्दामा उनी ११ पटकसम्म पक्राउ परिसकेका छन् ।

२०७१ सालमा अपहरण तथा शरीर बन्धक मुद्दामा दोषी ठहर भएपछि उनले लामो जेल सजाय भुक्तान गरेका थिए । कारागारबाट छुटेपछि उनी सामाजिक र राजनीतिक गतिविधिमा समेत सक्रिय बने । तर, पछिल्ला घटनाक्रमले उनको पुनः आपराधिक गतिविधिसँग सम्बन्ध रहेको आरोपलाई प्रहरीले गम्भीर रूपमा अनुसन्धान गरिरहेको छ ।

अनुसन्धान अझै जारी रहेकाले उनीमाथि लागेको आरोप अदालतबाट प्रमाणित भइसकेको अवस्था भने होइन । अब प्रहरी अनुसन्धान र अदालतको अन्तिम निर्णयले अभिषेक गिरीको कर्तुतको नयाँ पर्दाफास हुनेछ ।

articles.title: अपरेसन चार्लीबाट खुलेको रहस्य, नक्कली नोट छाप्ने गिरोह पक्राउ
articles.summary:
रुपन्देही । रुपन्देही प्रहरीले नक्कली नेपाली नोट, नोट छाप्न प्रयोग गरिएका उपकरण र त्यसमा संलग्न मानिसहरुलाई पक्राउ गरी सार्वजनिक गरेको छ । जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय भैरहवामा बुधबार पत्रकार सम्मेलन गरी प्रहरीले उक्त कार्यमा संलग्नहरु बारे जानकारी दिएको हो ।

रुपन्देही प्रहरीले नक्कली नोट, छाप्ने मेसिनरी उपकरणसहित ६ जनालाई पक्राउ गरेको छ । असार २६ गते बुटवलमा चिनजानकै गंगा कुमारी पुर्वछानेले एक महिलालाई इसेवामार्फत् २ हजार १ सय रुपैयाँ ट्रान्सफर गर्न लगाएर दुईवटा हजारका नोट दिएकी थिइन् ।

पछि ती नोट नक्कली भएको थाहा पाएपछि पीडित महिलाले इलाका प्रहरी कार्यालय बुटवलमा निवेदन दिएकी थिइन् । पूर्वछानेलाई नियन्त्रणमा लिएर अनुसन्धान गर्ने क्रममा नक्कली नोट, छाप्ने मेसिनरी उपकरणसहित प्रहरीले ६ जनालाई पक्राउ गरेको हो ।

अनुसन्धानका क्रममा बुटवल र पोखराका आरोपीहरुका घरबाट समेत नक्कली एक हजार दरका नोट प्रहरीले बरामद गरेको छ ।

डीएसपी चन्दका अनुसार पक्राउ पर्नेमा रुपन्देहीको बुटवल

उपमहानगरपालिका–११, सिर्जनानगर बस्ने बर्ष ३६ की गंगा कुमारी पुर्वछाने, कास्कीको पोखरा महानगरपालिका–१ बस्ने कृष्ण भन्ने किरण कृष्ण तिवारी, भक्तपुरको चाँगुनारायण नगरपालिका–१ बस्ने रामचन्द्र खत्री, कपिलवस्तुको बाणगंगा नगरपालालिका–२ बस्ने संजय थारु, दोलखाको सैलुङ गाउँपालिका–४ वस्ने वर्ष ३८ को पासाङ तामाङ र भारत पश्चिम बंगाल सिलुगुढी भक्तिनगर थाना बस्ने वर्ष ४९ को बासुमित्र आनन्द रहेका छन् ।

उनीहरुको घर तथा शरीर खानतलासीको क्रममा तयार भएका सक्कली जस्तो देखिने एक हजार दरका नक्कली नेपाली नोट ६ सय २२ थान बरामद गरिएको डीएसपी चन्दले बताए ।

प्रहरी फोटोकपी मेसिन, डेल कम्पनीको ल्याप्टप, नक्कली नोट कटिङ गर्न प्रयोग हुने मेसिन, नक्कली नोट प्रिन्ट गर्न प्रयोग हुने प्रिन्टर, नक्कली नोट छाप्न प्रयोग गर्ने पेपर १ कार्टुन पनि बरामद गरेको छ ।

यस्तै, नक्कली नोट बनाउन प्रयोग हुने केमिकल, लेमिलेसन मेसिन, प्लाष्टिक पेपर र ६ वटा मोबाइल पनि प्रहरीले बरामद गरेको छ ।

पीडित महिलाको निवेदनका आधारमा लुम्बिनी प्रदेश प्रहरी कार्यालय दाङ, जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय र इलका प्रहरी कार्यालय बुटवलले ‘अपरेसन चार्ली’ नाम दिएर नक्कली नोट सम्बन्धी संयुक्त अनुसन्धान सुरु गरेका थिए ।

पक्राउ गरेमा ६ जनाविरुद्ध रुपन्देही जिल्ला अदालतबाट मुद्रा सम्बन्धी कसूरमा ५ दिनको म्याद थप गरी अनुसन्धान जारी राखिएको प्रहरीे जनाएको छ । रुपन्देहीमा यसअघि पनि लुम्बिनी, सालझण्डी र बुटवलमै नक्कली नोट बरामद भएका थिए ।

articles.title: गृहमन्त्रीको आश्वासनपछि तेस्रो वार्ताको पखाईमा मिटरब्याजपीडित
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । प्रधानमन्त्री एवम् रास्वपा बरिष्ठ नेता बालेन्द्र शाहले न्याय खोज्न कोही पनि काठमाडौं जानु नपर्ने, काठमाडौं घुम्न र पशुपतिको दर्शन गर्न मात्रै जाने अवस्था आउने भनी मधेस प्रदेशमै गएर आश्वासन दिएका थिए ।

रास्वपालाई मधेसबाट जनताले भारी मत दिएर जिताए पनि ।तर प्रधानमन्त्री शाहले भनेजस्तो न्याय नपाएपछि न्याय खोज्न मिटरब्याज पीडितको एक समूहले जनकपुरबाट काठमाडौंका लािग पैदल यात्रा अघि बढायो।

पटक पटकको सहमति कार्यान्वयन नभएपछि आजित भएका उनीहरु निर्णायक आन्दोलन शुरु गरेका हुन् ।यसपाली जनकपुरबाट बाराको निजगढ आइपुग्दा गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङले आश्वासनको पोको फुकाएका छन् ।

न्यायको माग गर्दै जनकपुरबाट असार २५ गते सुरु भएको मिटरब्याज पीडितको पैदलयात्रा मंगलबार छैटौं दिन बाराको निजगढ आइपुग्यो । काठमाडौंतर्फ अघि बढ्दै गरेको उनीहरुको यात्रा भने निजगढमै रोकिएको छ ।

गृहमन्त्री सुधन गुरुङ मंगलबार निजगढ पुगेर उक्त समूहसँग वार्ता गरि माग पूरा गर्ने आश्वास दिएपछि यात्रा रोकिएको हो । गृहमन्त्री गुरुङले पीडितको माग पूरा गर्न ३ दिनको समय मागेपछि उनीहरु निजगढमै रोकिएका हुन् । तर माग पूरा नभए उनीहरुको यात्रा पुनः काठमाडौंतर्फ अघि बढ्नेछ ।

पीडितहरूले तमसुक व्यवस्था खारेज गर्न, मिटरब्याजसम्बन्धी विशेष ऐन ल्याउन, मिटरब्याजका नाममा गुमेको चल–अचल सम्पत्ति फिर्ता गराउन तथा दोषीमाथि कानुनी कारबाही गर्न आफनो सरकारसँग माग गरिरहेका छन् ।

२०७९ सालदेखि निरन्तर राज्यको ढोका ढक्ढकाउँदै आएका पीडितहरुले मिटरब्याज नियन्त्रणका लागि बनेका कानुन, कार्यविधि तथा सरकारसँग भएका सम्झौताहरू प्रभावकारी रूपमा कार्यान्वयन नभएपछि पुनः आन्दोलनको बाटो रोजेका हुन् । यसअघि उनीहरु दुई दुई पटक काठमाडौं आएर सरकारसँग सहमति गरेका थिए ।

मिटरब्याज पीडितको पैदलमार्चको श्रृङ्गखला

पहिलो पैदल मार्च

मिटरब्याज पीडित पहिलो पटक २०७९ चैत २ गते महोत्तरीको बर्दिबासबाट पैदल मार्चपास गर्दै काठमाडौं आएका थिए ।बर्दिबासबाट निस्किएका मधेशका ७२ जना मिटरब्याज पीडित ११ दिनमा काठमाडौं आईपुगेका थिए।आन्दोलन चर्की पछि चैत १८ गते सरकार र आन्दोलनकारी बिच पाँच बुँदे सहमति भयो।त्यस बेला पुष्पकमल दाहाल प्रचण्ड प्रधानमन्त्री थिए।सहमति अनुसार सरकारले विशेष अदालतका पूर्वअध्यक्ष गौरीबहादुर कार्कीको नेतृत्वमा जाँचबुझ आयोग गठन गर्यो।

सो आयोगमा २८ हजार भन्दा बढी उजुरी परे।पिडितको संख्या ठूलो भएपनि आयोगको म्याद सकिदाँ सम्म न्याय भने एकदम कम मात्रले पाए।जसमा १५ हजार उजुरीमाथि छानबिन भए पनि ५ हजार ५०० फस्र्यौट भएको थियो।तर अधिकांशमा भने कुनै सुनुवाई नै भएन।

दोस्रो पैदल मार्च

पहिलो पैदल मार्च भएको एक बर्ष नबित्दै मिटर ब्याज पिडित फेरि काठमाडौंमा लागि निस्किए । २०८० माघ १६ गते मेची र महाकालीबाट एकैपटक मिटरब्याज तथा ठगी बिरुद्ध पिडितहरुको पैदल मार्च निस्कियो । दोस्रो पैदल मार्चमा करिब ४ सयको संख्यामा पिडित सहभागी थिए ।

काठमाडौंमा उनीहरुको सशंक्त आन्दोलनपछि २०८० फागुन २८ गते फेरि सरकार र मिटरब्याज पिडित बिच वार्ता भइ अर्को चार बुँदे सहमति भयो ।

दोस्रो सहमतिपछि २०८० चैत ९ गते सरकारले पुनः पूर्वन्यायाधीश तेजबहादुर कार्कीको नेतृत्वमा अर्को मिटरब्याजसम्बन्धी जाँचबुझ आयोग गठन ग¥यो । तेजबहादुर नेतृत्वको आयोगमा ३२ हजार उजुरी प¥यो । तर, सबैको प्रभावकारी सुनुवाई हुन सकेन ।

आयोगको काम प्रभाकारी नभएपछि पडितले संघर्ष जारी नै राखे ।पुनः २०८१ फागुन २८ गते सरकारले पूर्व न्यायाधीश बाबुराम रेग्मीको अध्यक्षतामा अर्को तीन सदस्यीय अनुचित लेनदेनसम्बन्धी जाँचबुझ आयोग बनायो ।तेस्रो पटक गठन भएको यो आयोगमा पनि करिब १० हजार उजुरी परे । तर कार्यान्वयन भएन ।

यी आयोगहरू गठन हुनुअघि २०७९ असोज १ गते पनि सरकारले गृह मन्त्रालयका अधिकारी भीष्मराज भुषालको नेतृत्वमा मिटरब्याज अपराध नियन्त्रण सिफारिस कार्यदल गठन भएको थियो । यसपछि मिटरब्याज पीडितहरूले जिल्ला प्रशासन कार्यालयमा उजुरी दिएका थिए । तर केहीको उजुरी सुनुवाई भएपनि अधिकांशको उजुरीको सुनुवाई नै भएन ।

तेस्रो पैदल मार्च

मिटरब्याज पीडितको तेस्रो पैदल मार्च गत असार २५ गते जनपुरको तिरहुतियागाछीबाट सुरु भएको हो । ३५ जिल्लाका चार सय भन्दा बढी पिडित सहभागी यो यात्रा १५ दिनमा काठमाडौं आइपुग्ने योजना थियो । सरकारले यसअघि सहमति गरि पटक पटक आयोग गठन गरि काम शुरु गरे पनि पूर्णता नदिएपछि उनीहरु आन्दोलित भएका हुन् । निजगढमा रोकिएको उनीहरुको यात्रा माग पूरा नभएपछि तीन दिनपछि पुनः काठमाडौं तर्फ अघि बढ्नेछ ।

मिटरब्याज पीडितको अन्त्यहीन संघर्ष

यसअघि दुइ पटक काठमाडौं सम्मको पैदलमार्च, संघीय सरकारसँग पटक पटक सहमति र तीन तीन वटा आयोग गठन। तर मिटरब्याज पीडितका समस्या ज्युका त्युँ। अनि कहिले प्रचण्ड गर्मी त कहीले झरीका बीच काठमाडौं तर्फको पैदल मार्च ।

मिटरब्याज पीडितहरु यो संघर्षको श्रृखंला माग पूरा नभएसम्म नरोक्ने योजनामा छन् । सरकारसँग पटक पटक सहमति हुने तर कार्यान्यन नहुदाँ उनीहरु पटक पटक आन्दोलनमा उत्रिन बाध्य भएका छन् । मिटरब्याज समस्या समाधानका लागि गृहमन्त्री गुरुङ समक्ष प्रस्तुत गरेका ६ बुँदे मागमाथि प्रधानमन्त्री कार्यालयमा छलफलको क्रममा छ ।

अब प्रधानमन्त्री कार्यालयको निर्णय आएपछि गृहमन्त्री र मिटरब्याजविरुद्ध किसान–मजदुर आन्दोलनको नेतृत्वबीच पुनः तेस्रो चरणको वार्ता हुनेछ ।

articles.title: How video calls have become the new daily ritual for lonely Nepali parents
articles.summary:
Every evening, Kamal Nath Dahal waits for the same thing.

It is not a visitor at his door. It is not the sound of footsteps in his hallway.

It is the glow of a mobile phone screen.

When his sons, daughters-in-law and three-year-old granddaughter appear on the screen from Japan, the quiet room where he lives alone in Kathmandu suddenly feels less empty.

For a few minutes, the distance between Nepal and Japan disappears.

Dahal asks about their day. He watches his granddaughter’s expressions. He listens to his sons’ voices.

Then the call ends, and the silence returns.

The 68-year-old from Melamchi, Sindhupalchok, has built a routine around that silence. Each morning, he performs his prayers, prepares his meals, reads books, listens to the news and goes about his work.

“Work is the one thing that keeps my mind busy,” he said.

But staying occupied does not erase the feeling of missing his family.

“We talk on the phone a lot. I know everything happening in their lives. But the happiness of sitting together in Nepal, eating whatever is cooked in the same kitchen, cannot be compared with a video call.”

For Dahal, the hardest moments come during festivals.

“When you see everyone gathering with their families, you wonder how wonderful it would have been if my sons were here with me,” he said.

Yet the same technology that reminds him of the distance also helps him endure it.

“The mobile phone has become like a god for people like us. It brings distant people close,” he said.

The phone has also become a way for him to preserve a connection with his granddaughter, who was born in Japan and is growing up far from Nepal.

Whenever she appears on screen, Dahal asks her the same question.

“Say ‘Ba’,” he tells her.

The little girl responds.

He has taught her other Nepali words too—“Aama” (mother), “Kaka” (uncle) and “Kaki” (aunt). He worries that children growing up abroad may lose their connection to their family’s language and culture.

“Wherever children live, I want them to remember their country and their language,” he said.

His sons have invited him to visit Japan several times, but he has not been able to go.

His bigger hope is different: that one day they return home.

“Foreign countries are places to learn, not places to spend your entire life,” he said. “Work there, gain experience, but invest in your own country.”

For now, the phone screen is his window into the lives of the people he loves.

But his real wish remains unchanged.

“One day, I hope my sons return to Nepal permanently, and we can sit together in the same kitchen and eat again.”

Dahal’s story is becoming increasingly common.

As thousands of young Nepalis leave for education, employment and better opportunities abroad, many parents are growing older in homes where their children’s voices now arrive through a screen.

In Pokhara’s Ratnachowk neighbourhood, 69-year-old Saraswati Maharjan lives among reminders of the family she misses.

Photographs of her parents, daughters, sons-in-law and grandchildren cover the walls of one room in her two-storey house.

Her elder daughter has lived in Japan for 13 years. Her younger daughter lives in Janakpur.

Although one daughter is still in Nepal, Saraswati says distance can exist even within the same country.

“When my elder daughter came from Japan, my younger daughter also came to meet her,” she said. “Even though she is in Nepal, it feels like she is abroad. She has not come since.”

Her husband, once a chef at a Pokhara hotel, suffered a health emergency several years ago. Both daughters returned during his treatment, but eventually left again.

Today, he can walk around the house but has lost his ability to speak.

“Earlier, we would spend time talking together. Sometimes we would go out during fairs and festivals,” Saraswati said. “That is no longer possible.”

Technology helps her stay connected with her daughters.

The family has a Messenger group where they regularly talk through video calls.

“I do not feel like my daughters are far away,” she said.

But festivals remain painful.

“Dashain, Tihar and Teej are the hardest,” she said. “When daughters and relatives return to everyone else’s homes, my house feels empty.”

Still, she understands why her daughters left.

“We struggled to educate our children,” she said. “Once they studied and grew wings, we had to let them fly.”

For Hari and Mina Gurung (names changed), the empty spaces left behind by migration have become part of daily life.

The couple, aged 64 and 61, have lived alone in Kathmandu’s Tokha area for nine years.

Their daughters moved to Australia, one for higher education and another for work.

Hari once encouraged them to leave, believing foreign education would create opportunities.

Today, he understands the cost.

“At that time, we thought studying abroad would give our children better opportunities,” he said. “But after finishing their studies, they begin thinking about settling permanently. That leaves you with a strange emptiness.”

Their days now follow a quiet rhythm—morning walks, exercise, newspapers, household chores, gardening and caring for chickens.

Their daughters remain close through regular calls.

“They call us, send voice messages and leave messages,” Hari said. “That alone reassures us.”

But Mina says the absence becomes more frightening during illness.

“When we were alone, we worried about what would happen if both of us fell sick at the same time and our children were not around,” she said.

Not every parent experiences distance as a loss.

For 63-year-old Dr Samjhana Dhakal of Kupandol, Lalitpur, her son’s life abroad is something she accepts.

Her son lives in Scotland, but daily conversations have kept their relationship strong.

“I speak with my son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren every day,” she said. “Technology has made the world much smaller.”

Dhakal believes parents must allow their children to pursue their futures, even when that means living far away.

“As parents, we cannot think only about wanting them beside us,” she said. “A child’s progress is the greatest happiness for a parent.”

Having lived abroad herself for education, she understands the choices her son made.

For many Nepali parents, migration has created a new reality.

Their children may be thousands of kilometres away, but they remain only a phone call away.

Technology has shortened the distance.

But for parents like Dahal, the dream is still simple: not another video call, but a family meal at the same table, in the same kitchen, once again.

When children and families live far apart, their relationships are likely to weaken, says Laxman Prasad Sharma, Associate Professor of Sociology at Tribhuvan University. While technology allows parents in Nepal to stay in touch with children living abroad through video calls and messaging apps, he argues that digital communication cannot preserve the emotional closeness that comes from living together.

Technology may create the impression that families remain connected, Sharma says, but “social, family and emotional relationships have become increasingly fragile as migration has grown.” Beyond physical distance, he warns, prolonged separation weakens family intimacy, disrupts the transfer of cultural values between generations, and shapes how children are raised and socialised—processes he considers fundamental to a healthy society.

Although Sharma acknowledges the benefits of technology, he believes it cannot replace face-to-face interaction. “Technology can be a tool for building a modern society, but it cannot be an end in itself,” he says.

articles.title: Lawmakers seek tougher Everest climbing rules with 263 amendments to Tourism Bill
articles.summary:
Several lawmakers have proposed significantly tightening the qualifications required to climb Mount Everest as Nepal’s Integrated Tourism Bill enters a parliamentary committee for clause-by-clause scrutiny.

A total of 58 lawmakers have registered 263 amendments to the bill before it returns to Parliament for final debate and voting.

Although the proposals differ in detail, they share a common objective: requiring climbers to prove their experience on lower peaks before being allowed to attempt the world’s highest mountain.

Lawmakers Shishir Khadka and Nitima Bhandari Karki have proposed issuing Everest permits only to climbers who have successfully climbed at least one mountain above 7,000 metres and two mountains above 8,000 metres in Nepal.

They have also proposed that all commercial mountaineering activities, expedition promotion and marketing, and the sale of expedition packages be carried out only through trekking agencies registered and licensed in Nepal.

“Foreign companies shall not be permitted to directly sell or operate such expeditions or packages,” their proposed amendment states.

The lawmakers have further proposed that the government determine the carrying capacity of each mountain before opening it for climbing.

“When opening any mountain in Nepal for climbing, the government shall determine the maximum number of climbers permitted on each mountain during every climbing season after considering the mountain’s physical carrying capacity, favourable weather windows, and the level of congestion likely to occur,” the proposal says.

It also recommends auctioning climbing permits within the prescribed quota by setting a minimum price and awarding the permits to the highest bidders.

Lawmaker Ganesh Karki has proposed that Everest permits be issued only after applicants provide documentary proof of successfully climbing at least one mountain above 7,000 metres and one above 8,000 metres in Nepal.

Similarly, lawmaker Ganesh Bahadur Bishwakarma has proposed mandatory mountaineering training and medical certification for all applicants. Climbers would have to submit certificates from recognised mountaineering training institutions and a government-recognised health facility, based on a medical examination conducted within one month of the application.

Bishwakarma has also proposed requiring proof of a successful ascent of at least one mountain above 7,000 metres in Nepal before an Everest permit is issued.

Lawmaker Dhananjaya Regmi has proposed that climbers seeking permits for mountains above 8,000 metres first demonstrate successful ascents of at least two peaks above 6,000 metres and one above 7,000 metres in Nepal.

Several lawmakers have also proposed that climbing permits for any 8,000-metre peak, not just Everest, be issued only after applicants successfully climb at least one mountain above 7,000 metres in Nepal.

Another proposal recommends that all climbers and expedition members complete the full acclimatisation process within Nepal before attempting a summit.

Lawmaker Bodha Narayan Shrestha has proposed that government-appointed liaison officers be provided salaries, allowances, accommodation, food and other benefits by the state. Currently, these costs are borne by expedition teams.

Lawmakers have also proposed allocating designated plots for base camps and higher camps and allowing camps to be established only in approved areas.

Another amendment seeks to establish integrated check posts for mountaineering management, headed by a Nepali Army officer and staffed by representatives of relevant government agencies. Liaison officers would be deployed at these posts in sufficient numbers to monitor climbing activities and would be required to reside there.

Adventure tourism activities such as paragliding, skydiving, heli-skiing and ultralight flying during climbing expeditions would be permitted only on mountains below 6,000 metres.

The proposals also call for the creation of a permanent Tourism Crisis Management and Recovery Fund to support the tourism industry during pandemics, natural disasters and other crises. The fund would provide wage support for tourism workers, concessional refinancing and soft loans, with a fixed percentage of tourism taxes or royalties earmarked for the fund.

Lawmakers have proposed that all personnel involved in mountaineering operations—including Sirdars, mountain guides, climbing support staff, cooks, videographers and photographers—must be Nepali citizens.

They also propose that taxes be deducted at source from workers’ wages, deposited against their permanent account numbers (PAN), and that all payments be made through Nepali banks.

Above base camp, climbing support workers would be prohibited from carrying more than 20 kilograms of equipment or supplies.

The proposals also guarantee that Sirdars, mountain guides and climbing support workers may refuse to continue an expedition if weather conditions become hazardous, their health deteriorates, or their safety is at risk. Workers exercising this right would be protected from wage deductions, dismissal or other employment-related penalties.

Insurance requirements would also be significantly strengthened. The proposals call for a mandatory cashless medical and rescue insurance scheme meeting international standards.

Insurance coverage for climbing support workers, Sirdars and mountain guides would be based on prevailing market values and occupational risks, with minimum coverage of Rs50 million in the event of death, Rs20 million for medical treatment and Rs10 million for search and rescue. Parliament would review these coverage amounts every three years.

Every expedition would also be required to obtain insurance from a licensed Nepali insurer covering personal accidents, medical treatment, search and rescue, and the management and transportation of mortal remains.

Environmental provisions include a ban on single-use plastics in all mountaineering areas and the implementation of a zero-waste policy for both biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste.

Under another proposal, every expedition team would be required to digitally track or QR-code every item carried onto the mountain, record all equipment transported above base camp, and weigh and certify all equipment and human waste brought back before returning it to base camp.

The amendments also propose banning drones and helicopters above 6,000 metres without prior government approval, except for national security or other authorised purposes.

No Sirdar, mountain guide, high-altitude worker or base camp worker would be allowed to accompany an expedition unless they are members of a recognised mountaineering association.

Lawmakers have also proposed making licensed guides mandatory on designated high-risk, protected, Himalayan and remote trekking routes, including climbing expeditions.

The bill also seeks tighter regulation of digital tourism platforms. Under the proposal, all online tourism service providers offering booking, marketing, listing or facilitation services in Nepal would be required to register with the Department of Tourism.

Foreign digital tourism platforms operating in Nepal would have to appoint a local representative, register for tax, set up a consumer grievance mechanism, and regularly submit business reports. Licensed Nepali tourism service providers could be barred from using unregistered digital platforms.

The National Assembly passed the Integrated Tourism Bill on February 9. The legislation aims to diversify and systematically regulate Nepal’s tourism sector while strengthening safety, environmental and governance standards in mountaineering.

articles.title: Government’s digital services buckle under repeated system failures
articles.summary:
At 85 years old, Sabitri Devi Udas, accompanied by her husband, made her way to the ward 31 office of the Kathmandu Metropolitan City in Shantinagar at 11 am on Monday. The new fiscal year had just commenced, and elderly citizens were flocking to local ward offices to renew their social security allowance identity cards. When she inquired about the renewal process, a municipal official offered a familiar, disheartening refrain: ‘The system [server] is down.’

Hoping the system would come back online, she stayed put. Every so often, she walked to the counter and asked, "Has the system started working?" Each time, the staff shook their heads: "Not yet, mother." By 3 pm, after four hours of fruitless waiting, she had run out of patience. "What kind of system is this that cannot be restored even after hours?" she lamented. It was her second fruitless trip to the ward office for a simple administrative procedure, having spent hours there on Friday under identical circumstances.

Seventy-eight-year-old Narwada Devi Sharma, who came from Old Baneshwar alongside her two daughters, faced much the same ordeal. Suffering from severe knee joint pain that makes mobility painful, waiting all day in an overcrowded office proved agonising. "We stayed hoping the work would get done," she said. "After waiting for four hours, they simply told us to go home and return another day. I don’t know when I will be able to manage another trip, as I cannot travel alone and must coordinate with family members."

The plight of these elderly citizens exposes the massive gulf between the official rhetoric of digital governance and the ground reality across the country. For years, successive administrations have touted the vision of a ‘Digital Nepal’, promising that migrating public services online—ranging from digital land records, e-payment portals, and online application forms to digital mapping and electronic asset-freezing systems—would eliminate middlemen, bolster transparency, and end the necessity of standing in physical queues.

These promises were renewed recently when the newly formed government led by Balendra Shah released a 100-point priority checklist for administrative reform. The roadmap placed high priority on advancing government digitisation and expanding information technology (IT) adoption. In practice, however, systemic failures are producing the opposite effect, severely disrupting access at heavily frequented public portals such as land revenue offices, transport management centres, the Department of National ID and Civil Registration, and local municipal wards.

The Ministry of Women, Children, and Senior Citizens recently directed all local governments to renew social security allowance identity cards. It also required beneficiaries whose biometric details had already been recorded to appear in person for verification. The circular instructed local units to verify individuals via fingerprint or facial recognition. Although central directives clarified that mandatory biometric re-verification should not be forced on those already registered, local units have insisted on physical re-verification. As a result, elderly citizens arrive only to be turned away after waiting hours because the system crashes under the heavy load.

Bijaya Kumari Prasai, director at the Department of National ID and Civil Registration, clarified that local units were expressly advised against forcing unnecessary biometric steps on individuals whose profiles are already verified.

"We instructed local authorities that once an individual's biometric profile exists, a simple verification of life suffices, and if biometrics fail to capture, staff should log it as a technical exception," said Prasai. "Biometric verification was once compulsory, but that is no longer the case. The current problem stems from local authorities insisting on mandatory biometrics despite our guidelines."

However, a frontline official at the Kathmandu ward 31 office defended the practice, citing fears of administrative audits.

"If we don’t capture live biometrics, auditors later question why it was skipped," said the ward official anonymously. "Therefore, we insist on mandatory biometrics. If the server fails today, we simply ask citizens to return another day,” she added.

The systemic breakdown extends far beyond local ward offices. At the Transport Management Service Office in Sallaghari, Bhaktapur, Bhagawati Phuyal arrived on Monday on her scooter to renew her vehicle ownership document (bill book). Upon reaching the entrance, security guards directed her to a notice on the gate. "The system is offline today," they told her.

"I came here last Friday, and the office was practically deserted with hardly any staff present," said Phuyal. "Today the staff are present, but the system is down. My bill book renewal deadline expired at the end of the last fiscal year, and I am running out of options."

Nearby stood Sunil Parajuli, a driver who transports Chinese tourists. He had taken time off work to visit the transport office for the second time in three days.

"I came a few days ago, and no work could be done. Today is no different," said Parajuli. "Making repeated trips back and forth without achieving anything is deeply frustrating."

The notice at the transport office gate cited ‘database migration’ and “structural realignments” of vehicle registration records to comply with the new fiscal budget provisions. The Department of Transport Management requested service seekers not to visit its offices until July 24 except in emergencies, stating that the technical adjustments would take about a week.

Keshab Khatiwada, director at the Department of Transport Management, defended the disruption, stating that non-essential operations had to be paused across provinces to adjust internal software to new financial legislation.

"We are updating backend software to implement legal provisions related to tax rates and revenue collection," said Khatiwada. "Services haven’t been suspended nationwide. Offices in Lumbini province are functional, and emergency services continue uninterrupted elsewhere."

Similar breakdowns have plagued the country's land administration. At the end of the previous fiscal year, repeated crashes of the Public Access Module operated by the Department of Land Management and Archive paralysed land revenue offices nationwide. The crash stalled electronic request forms used by legal practitioners and financial institutions, disrupting land transfers, property freezes, and mortgage clearances.

Hari Sharan Thapa, a computer officer at the department, attributed the crash to the surge in transactions at the end of the fiscal year, which overloaded the server. He said the system has since stabilised, though acknowledging that fixing one software glitch frequently triggers another.

Technology experts argue that these chronic failures stem from fundamental architectural flaws and chronic underinvestment in IT maintenance. Manohar Kumar Bhattarai, a prominent electronic governance and IT expert, pointed out that public software infrastructure is rarely designed to handle peak traffic.

"Every public system experiences peak operational hours, and system architecture must be designed to anticipate traffic spikes," said Bhattarai. "Cloud-based infrastructure should possess auto-scaling capabilities that dynamically expand capacity when user traffic swells. However, Nepal's current public systems lack this basic flexibility and scalable capacity."

Bhattarai added that the root problem lies in poor procurement and planning rather than aging hardware alone. "Government agencies focus overwhelmingly on procurement procedures rather than long-term planning and the overall lifecycle of IT systems," said Bhattarai. "Contractual agreements fail to hold vendors accountable for system uptime. Furthermore, due to budget constraints and delays in foreign currency allocations, agencies often fail to purchase timely security patches, leaving software vulnerable."

According to officials at the Civil Registration Department, 6,743 local wards across the country attempt to log into the central system simultaneously between 10:30 am and 2:30 pm every day to process social security renewals, and this overloads the server.

Infrastructure across critical government data centres has gone without major upgrades for over three to four years, with many offices relying on outdated servers and software that lack regular security audits or Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) certificate updates.

The operational confusion has been compounded by recent structural overhauls within the bureaucracy. In March, the government dissolved standalone IT oversight bodies—including the Department of Information Technology and the Integrated Data Management Centre—transferring digital infrastructure, software management, and IT security mandates directly under the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers to reduce institutional fragmentation.

However, the theoretical benefits of this restructuring remain unrealised, as Organisation and Management (O&M) surveys have yet to be finalised.

Experts stress that administrative restructuring alone will not solve the crisis without technical capacity and sustained funding. "Transitioning to paperless governance requires far more than political declarations," said Bhattarai, suggesting that the government must invest equally in robust technical management, infrastructure scaling, and operational maintenance if digital public services are ever to become reliable.

The story has been updated.

articles.title: Ambassadorial selection in final stretch
articles.summary:
The selection process for new ambassadors, which began a month and a half ago, has entered its final stage, with the foreign minister expected to make recommendations next week.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs had on May 28 invited applications through an open call to fill vacant envoy positions in 13 countries, including India, China, the US, the UK, and Australia, and set June 5 as the deadline. More than 4,400 applications were received. After removing duplicate and incomplete applications, officials selected 2,700 before shortlisting a few hundred applications.

The shortlist was forwarded to Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal’s secretariat for final consideration.

“Shortlisting was a Herculean task as one individual had submitted 94 applications through email and post,” an official involved in the vetting process told the Post. He said Khanal was reviewing the CVs of prospective candidates, and recommendations for some ambassadorial appointments are expected to be made next week, said the official at the foreign ministry.

The final decision on the appointments will be taken after discussions among Prime Minister Balendra Shah, Rastriya Swatantra Party chief Rabi Lamichhane, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, and other top leaders of the ruling party. “However, our party is clear that the responsibility for the appointment solely rests with the government and the foreign minister,” said an RSP leader.

As the government expedites the selection process, prospective candidates have initiated intense lobbying with various power centres and the ruling RSP. Stating that such lobbying would have no influence on the appointment process, an RSP office bearer said, “They should be based on merit, and the right person should get the opportunity.”

Some missions have remained vacant since October last year. On October 16, the Sushila Karki-led government recalled Nepal’s ambassadors to China, Germany, Israel, Malaysia, Qatar, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Spain, the US, the UK, and Japan. Around a week after assuming office, the Shah government on April 7 recalled six more ambassadors—Shankar Prasad Sharma (India), Chitralekha Yadav (Australia), Purna Bahadur Nepali (Sri Lanka), Shiva Maya Tumbahangphe (South Korea), Sumnima Tuladhar (Denmark), and Kapil Shrestha (South Africa).

“The government appears less concerned about appointing ambassadors despite enjoying a strong political mandate,” said a Nepali diplomat.

Most of the missions, including those whose ambassadors were recalled by the current government in April, are being run by chargés d'affaires.

“Without a resident ambassador, an embassy can do little more than keep the office running,” said Naresh Bikram Dhakal, who served as Nepal’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia and Qatar. “If the government wants stronger political engagement and closer bilateral relations, it should appoint ambassadors without delay.”

Further delay in the appointments would leave more missions headless, as seven more ambassadors are retiring by the end of August. While the overwhelming number of applicants delayed the selection process, uncertainty over how many embassies the government planned to shut down also contributed to the delay. “Until the annual budget announcement, there was no clarity over how many missions would be shut down, so there was a kind of confusion. Now that confusion has been resolved,” a joint secretary at the foreign ministry said.

Through the budget, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle announced that the government would close the embassies in Denmark, Brazil, and South Africa, and shut down the Consulate General offices in San Francisco (US) and Chengdu (China), along with the embassy branch in Visakhapatnam (India).

“The foreign ministry therefore had to redraw its appointment plan, hence the delay,” the official said.

For decades, ambassadorial appointments have been divided between political nominees and career diplomats.

This time, the ministry invited applications through an open competition to fill ambassadorial posts in India, China, the US, the UK, Australia, Israel, South Korea, Austria, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Malaysia, Oman, and Saudi Arabia, among others, as well as positions at international organisations.

Talks are underway to give continuity to some ambassadors after they complete their terms after August, said one foreign ministry official. It is also not known whether recommendations will be made for the remaining seven missions after August.

“The selection process is under way,” said Lok Bahadur Paudel Chhetri, the foreign ministry spokesperson, adding, “Once it is complete, the recommendations will be made public.”

articles.title: Fertiliser crisis is hitting farmers hard. Fix it
articles.summary:
A shortage of chemical fertiliser during the peak farming season has been a perennial problem in Nepal. It recurred this year as well. The government has all the information regarding the quantity the country needs, the timing of the demand, and the investment required to make fertilisers available at subsidised prices. Yet, it persistently fails to ensure their timely availability. As a result, farmers, mainly from Tarai, have to rely on the Indian market, fraught with legal risks.

India provides fertilisers—mainly Di-Ammonium Phosphate (DAP), urea and potash—to its farmers at subsidised rates. Under India’s Fertiliser (Control) Order and the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, subsidised fertiliser distributed for agricultural use cannot legally be exported or transported outside the country without authorisation. The law enables authorities to confiscate both the fertiliser and the vehicle used for transportation, while offenders can face imprisonment and fines.

Indian security forces have often been flexible in allowing Nepali farmers to bring in a few sacks of fertiliser. However, rising prices and shortages triggered by global tensions have prompted the Indian states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar to tighten enforcement against attempts to supply fertiliser to Nepal. As a result, they are even making arrests, as recently happened to Nagendra Prasad Singh, 60, and Suresh Prasad Singh, 55, of Sarlahi district. The siblings, who were arrested in Sonbarsa, Bihar, remained behind bars for three weeks before the Nepal government started diplomatic dealings for their release.

Although it came late, the Foreign Ministry’s diplomatic initiative, which is expected to secure the release of the Singh brothers in a few days, is a welcome move. But that is not enough. Taking this as a lesson, the government should now focus on ensuring that no other Nepali citizen has to face what the Singh brothers endured. For that, chemical fertiliser should be made readily available to the nearly 60 percent of the population engaged in agriculture. Only then can the country permanently end the compulsion to depend on supplies from across the border.

Paddy production is not just a localised issue for farmers like the Singh brothers but a national concern, as it is directly linked to the country’s Gross Domestic Product. Better harvests contribute to higher economic growth, and fertiliser is one of the key inputs for increasing agricultural productivity. Nepali farmers are already struggling with several challenges. Less than half of the country’s agricultural land has irrigation facilities, leaving the rest dependent on rainfall. Erratic rainfall patterns caused by climate change have further compounded the problem. Expanding irrigation infrastructure is costly and time-consuming; climatic conditions are beyond anyone’s control.

One thing that any responsible government can address, however, is the timely availability of chemical fertiliser. This is possible through timely planning by assessing what volume of each type of fertiliser is needed and when. Successive governments have promised such planning but failed to deliver. As the present government came to power only about four months ago, it may not be appropriate to pin the blame on it. However, it cannot be excused if the same problem persists in the next planting season. The government’s ability to ensure the timely supply of fertiliser should be the basis for judging its performance.

articles.title: Raised $4 billion. Time for a new round
articles.summary:
A decade ago this summer, a 41-year-old economist stood among the architects of one of the fastest, most credible disaster assessments a poor country has ever produced. Nepal’s National Planning Commission (NPC) had one month to answer a pressing question after the 2015 earthquakes killed nearly 9,000 people: How much would it cost to rebuild and could the world be persuaded to pay for it?

Swarnim Wagle, then a member of the Commission, steered that process jointly with the World Bank, UNDP, the EU, ADB and JICA to deliver on June 15, 2015, a Post Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) which put the damage at roughly $7 billion and reconstruction needs at $6.7 billion, about 30 percent of GDP. Ten days later, at the International Conference on Nepal’s Reconstruction (ICNR), held under a tent in Tundikhel, the world answered. Over $4 billion was pledged, with India committing $1 billion, China $483 million, the World Bank $500 million and ADB $600 million.

It remains one of the more remarkable feats of economic diplomacy in Nepal’s modern history. This is why, when Wagle took oath as Finance Minister on March 27, so many people in Kathmandu’s business community allowed themselves a flicker of hope. Finally, here was a technocrat who had actually done the thing everyone talks about doing. He converted Nepal’s chronic credibility deficit into hard commitments from people who did not have to say yes.

The RSP’s near two-thirds majority in the March election meant that Nepal had, for once, the thing every economist says the country lacks: Political stability with a clear reform mandate and no coalition to appease. If ever there was a moment to convert legitimacy into capital, this was it.

On May 29, Wagle delivered the largest budget in Nepal’s history: Rs2,124.34 billion, targeting 7 percent growth up from 3.85 percent the year before. He doubled the income tax exemption threshold, cut the top marginal rate 10 points to 29 percent, simplified customs from 11 tariff tiers to seven, abolished excise duty on 360 goods and announced a sovereign wealth fund to deploy part of Nepal’s record $24 billion reserves. He proposed easier exit rules for foreign investors, a mechanism for Nepali firms to list on foreign exchanges through Global Depositary Receipts and a pledge to pursue new investment-protection and double-taxation treaties. On paper, it read like a market-friendly reset.

The market did not agree. In the first 100 days of the Balendra Shah government, the Nepal Stock Exchange fell on 45 of 67 trading days, sliding from a pre-inauguration high near 2,950 points to a six-month low around 2,570–a decline that continued even after the budget directly addressed long-standing investor demands. Nearly Rs600 billion in market value evaporated. Non-performing loans officially climbed to 5.6 percent. Private investment as a share of GDP fell from roughly a quarter to under a fifth. And most tellingly, by June, only 35 percent of the year’s capital budget had been spent, worse than the 44 percent managed by the previous government over the same period. A government elected explicitly to fix execution was executing worse than its predecessor.

Wagle, today, holds an interesting position, for he now has to cure the disease that he once diagnosed. As an opposition MP in April 2024, watching Nepal stage yet another underwhelming investment summit, he said plainly, “It’s been 30 years that Nepal has been asking foreigners to invest in Nepal. But they are not coming. Why should they come?”

He is now the man who has to answer his own question.

The PDNA playbook was built for sovereign-to-sovereign pledging: Governments and multilateral development banks committing grants and concessional loans against a public reconstruction bill that everyone had a humanitarian stake in closing. What Nepal needs now is a structurally different type of money—catalytic capital and commercial foreign direct investment. Providers of such capital only respond to measurable impact and risk-adjusted return.

Development Finance Institutions (DFIs), like IFC, the US Development Finance Corporation, British International Investment and ADB’s private-sector window, exist to provide catalytic capital to absorb early risk that commercial money won’t yet touch, proving out a market so others can follow. Nepal’s hydropower, agri-processing and climate-resilient infrastructure sectors are strong candidates as they are theoretically bankable. But there isn’t enough confidence among DFIs because of currency risk, uncertain offtake agreements, land acquisition friction, inconsistent policies and practices on the flow of foreign capital in and out of the country.

Multinational and regional private equity already active elsewhere in South Asia, portfolio investors and sovereign co-investors that are more commercially oriented want none of the development narrative. They want comparables. They want to see what has already worked in Nepal, what an exit actually looks like in practice and what an arbitration clause is worth when tested.

Wagle is uniquely equipped to speak to both audiences. His own 2011 World Bank research on FDI-specific regulation argued that what attracts FDI into a country is regulatory design, not the size of the tax break on offer. Few Nepali ministers could make that argument to a room of institutional investors in their own analytical language.

And there is no better time than now for Wagle to hit the road to showcase his vision for Nepal’s economic prosperity and ask international investors to commit their capital and resources to Nepal. Invite the hyper-scalers to set up ring-fenced 30 MW data centres alongside hydropower plants we have. Approach established infra builders specialising in building mega projects to commission rail networks to connect key cities under BOOT or HAM. Convene a marathon session with DFIs to improve their confidence to have them commit their capital for Nepali businesses in addition to the hydro and financial sectors.

Let’s not use geopolitics as an excuse to delay getting started. Given the clean governance and broader management bandwidth the new government brings to the table, coupled with Nepal’s superior brand equity, the perceived geo-political challenges should be manageable, especially with respect to our economic agenda.

Catalytic capital conversation should come before commercial roadshows in Singapore, Mumbai or Dubai, because early risk-absorption by development finance institutions is what makes the subsequent commercial pitch credible in the first place. Ideally, the newly proposed sovereign wealth fund should be positioned as a co-investment signal—evidence that Nepal is willing to put its own reserves alongside foreign capital.

And whatever gets negotiated needs an institutional home that survives the minister who negotiated it to ensure a delivery mechanism with statutory backing so that a cabinet reshuffle or the next election cycle does not strand half-built projects.

The continuity between Wagle’s two biggest tests, a decade apart, is the fact that his skill has always been producing numbers and arguments so rigorous that sceptical outsiders have no choice but to trust them. Can the man who previously raised $4 billion for a broken nation now persuade international private capital to invest in a politically stable Nepal brimming with potential?

articles.title: Debate on federalism should extend beyond politics
articles.summary:
Much of the debate on the relevance of Nepal’s provincial tier has focused on costs. However, the decision to establish provinces was never merely an economic or administrative one. It was fundamentally a political and constitutional response to Nepal’s long struggle for inclusion, representation and regional autonomy. The demand dates back to the establishment of the Nepal Tarai Congress in 1951. These movements ultimately shaped the federal structure enshrined in the 2015 Constitution.

Federalism, however, was intended to achieve more than political inclusion. It sought to constitutionally decentralise public authority, fiscal resources, planning and investment so that economic opportunities would spread beyond the Kathmandu Valley. Provinces should, therefore, be judged not only by political debates, but also by empirical evidence. Have Nepal’s development indicators improved during the federal era? While this alone cannot establish direct causation, it helps assess whether Nepal’s development trajectory has strengthened since federalism was implemented.

As political scientist Daniel Elazar described, federalism combines self-rule with shared rule, meaning provincial governments are constitutionally empowered entities rather than federal subordinates. Ronald Watts, a leading scholar of comparative federalism, noted that federalism brings governance closer to citizens to better reflect local priorities, while professor Wallace Oates explained that subnational governments deliver public services more efficiently due to superior local knowledge. Together, these frameworks show that provinces are meant to strengthen democracy, improve service delivery and foster long-term development. The central question remains whether this holds up in Nepal’s case.

To examine this, I compared key macroeconomic and fiscal indicators before and after provincial governments became operational, utilising data from the IMF’s World Economic Outlook Database (2024). To prevent distortion from extraordinary shocks, the earthquake years (2015-16), the transition year (2017) and the Covid-19 pandemic years (2020-21) were excluded. The analysis thus covers two stable periods: 2010-14 (pre-federal) and 2018-19 combined with 2022-24 (post-federal).

While weighted averages provide greater precision, simple arithmetic averages were used due to data limitations across all indicators. This descriptive approach offers transparency, though it should not be treated as a formal econometric assessment. The findings are encouraging. Every indicator moved positively during the post-federal period. Average annual real GDP growth rose from 4.49 percent to 5.0 percent, suggesting a stronger growth trajectory during comparable non-crisis years.

Recent fiscal data directly reinforces this transition. According to the Financial Comptroller General Office’s 2024-25 financial report across all three government tiers, capital spending accounts for 61 percent of total provincial expenditure compared to just 15 percent for the federal government and 35 percent at the local level. Although the provincial fiscal purse remains relatively small, this stark contrast underscores their primary focus on development and infrastructure investment. Taken together, these metrics confirm that Nepal achieved stronger macroeconomic and fiscal performance alongside provincial operations. At minimum, the evidence shows that federalism has coincided with an era of enhanced national development rather than economic stagnation.

While the national economic picture is encouraging, the regional reality remains mixed. A primary objective of federalism is not merely boosting aggregate national income, but distributing economic opportunities more equitably across provinces. In a mature federal system, subnational units should gradually emerge as self-sustaining centres of production, investment and employment rather than remaining peripheral to a single dominant metropolis.

Measured against this benchmark, progress has been slower than anticipated. According to the National Statistics Office’s recent GDP data set, Bagmati Province remains Nepal’s primary economic hub, accounting for 36.71 percent of national GDP. Though down marginally from 37.03 percent in 2018-19, this persistent concentration shows that nearly eight years of federal governance have yielded only a modest shift in regional economic balance.

There are, nevertheless, encouraging signs of dispersion. Gandaki (8.87percent to 8.98 percent), Lumbini (14.15 percent to 14.19 percent), Karnali (3.98 percent to 4.20 percent) and Sudurpashchim (6.86 percent to 7.03 percent)—each recorded slight gains in their national GDP share between 2018-19 and 2025-26. While small, these gains indicate that economic activity is slowly branching beyond the traditional capital core.

Contrarily, Koshi (15.81 percent to 15.80 percent) and Madhesh (13.30 percent to 13.08 percent) experienced a slight decline over the same period. The stagnation in Madhesh is particularly notable. Given its fertile agricultural plains, industrial clusters, proximity to the Indian border and central role in the political movement for federalism, Madhesh was widely expected to become a primary engine of regional growth. Its sluggish share suggests its full economic potential remains untapped.

Provincial fiscal space remains severely constrained. In Fiscal Year 2026-27, the combined budget of all seven provincial governments totals roughly Rs300 billion—a sum rivalled by single federal ministries, such as the Ministry of Infrastructure Development (approximately Rs310 billion). This stark imbalance underscores that despite constitutional devolution, development capital remains overwhelmingly centralised. Without expanded fiscal and administrative autonomy, provinces will struggle to meet their constitutional mandates.

While political debates often dominate discussions on federalism, its success ultimately hinges on economic outcomes. The evidence suggests that Nepal’s federal transition has coincided with stronger growth, higher capital investment and expanded fiscal capacity. Though provinces are not solely responsible for these gains, their focus on capital spending has strengthened state capacity at the grassroots level.

However, the economic promise of federalism remains partially unfulfilled. Economic activity remains heavily concentrated in Bagmati Province, while other provinces have made only modest gains. Moving forward, the core challenge facing Nepal is not whether provinces should exist, but how to transform them into powerful engines of regional development.

If the first decade of federalism was defined by constitutional setup and political devolution, the next must centre on economic federalism. This requires strengthening provincial economies, expanding their fiscal space, enacting delayed federal legislation, attracting regional investment and narrowing inter-provincial disparities.

Unlocking these potential demands stronger collaboration between provincial administrations and the private sector. Subnational governments must foster investment-friendly environments, while businesses need to look beyond the Kathmandu Valley, towards emerging regional markets. Simultaneously, national public investment and institutions must be strategically decentralised across the provinces to accelerate balanced growth.

articles.title: Why people are ordering fake food and fashion deliveries on free ‘dopamine apps’
articles.summary:
It’s Saturday night and you’ve downloaded a new food delivery app. You’ve scanned the menus, picked some Mexican dishes, placed your order and are now tracking the delivery. But your food never comes – and you never expected it to.

It sounds ridiculous if you’ve never tried it, but this viral trend is more popular than you might think. Just one app alone, FoodNeverComes, claims nearly 1 million “cravings satisfied” to date.

Why would people bother spending time on apps or websites that are built to never deliver? Ultimately, it’s all about getting a dopamine hit.

It sounds like harmless fun, letting users “buy” food, clothes or other products with no real-world cost, since most of these apps are free to use.
