But even when an app or website costs you nothing, there are downsides to watch out for – including how your choices can help advertisers better target you in real life.

From South Korea to the world

FoodNeverComes is one example of a free, ad-supported app and website that mimics an online food delivery service. But there are other types too.

For instance, the free, ad-supported Dopamine Shop is a fake online shopping site. There, customers view items – everything from a 99 cent pet rock to a $99 million moon – then fill their carts. But no payment details are requested and no transaction ever occurs. Nothing is ever shipped.

There are even fake, free “smoking” apps such as No Smoke Zone, also known as Virtual Smoke, which describes itself like this:

Virtual Smoke is a realistic cigarette simulation app that lets you enjoy the look, feel, and relaxation of smoking – without any nicotine or harmful effects. Perfect for those trying to quit, reduce stress, or just have fun with a virtual cigarette.

These new platforms are what’s known as “dopamine apps” or “dopamine sites”.

While they began in South Korea, interestingly, Dopamine Shop is owned and developed by Fenwick Holdings LLC, a small independent studio in the United States. This suggests this new genre of apps and websites may be spreading globally.

Why does it feel so good?

Dopamine is both a powerful neurotransmitter and neuromodulator – delivering chemical messages and sparking changes in your brain.

Dopamine plays several important roles, including motivating us toward goals and helping your brain learn which actions lead to beneficial outcomes.

With these new dopamine platforms, users experience:

The only element of the process missing, compared to a real app or website, is consumption (“I received it”).

Even before these latest apps, some people had already realised they can get a similar retail therapy rush by creating wish lists or filling their cart, then deleting it, without making a purchase.

You can simulate the same feeling by creating your dream home, without building a thing. Or you can imagine your dream holiday, using various free or paid travel planning apps and websites.

Potential as a ‘gateway behaviour’

Could pretending to order food, shopping or having “fun with a virtual cigarette” have any downsides?

These dopamine apps and websites are relatively new, so we don’t yet have specific research on how much, if at all, they might serve as “gateway behaviours”. A gateway behaviour is an initial behaviour that opens a pathway toward later behaviours becoming more likely.

However, this is an area that’s been well studied before in other areas, such as gambling and gaming. And that past research raises potential concerns – particularly since these dopamine apps involve some level of gamification.

For example, a notable 2014 study followed 409 people who played social casino games, but who had never gambled online with real money. Six months later, about 26% had migrated to real online gambling.

A 2016 study of 521 social casino users found 19% reported gambling for real money as a direct result of social casino gaming.

And a 2018 study of 1,178 German teens, aged 11 to 19, found that engagement with simulated gambling predicted subsequent real money gambling one year later.

How your ‘cookies’ feed targeted ads

Remember the old saying, “there’s no such thing as a free lunch”?

While these apps and websites might be fun and free, your fake choices can still be incredibly valuable for marketers.

Free apps often rely on advertising to pay for making their content free. Apps or websites that use Google AdSense to display their ads use cookies: tiny text files stored on your browser to track your online browsing habits.

Third-party advertisers, including Google, can then use your history to serve you more targeted ads. (If you read the fine print, sites note how to opt out of personalised advertising.)

If you do purchase that pretend jacket, or order that delivery of fake tacos, don’t be surprised if you start seeing more ads for the real thing.

articles.title: Everyday AI: Gunjan Dixit
articles.summary:
Beginning the research

I use AI at the beginning of the research process. It helps me identify possible themes, references, keywords and sources that I can explore further. Instead of asking it to complete the research for me, I use it to understand where I should begin and what questions I should be asking.

Preparing for a production

Before rehearsals begin, AI can help organise the early stages of thinking around a play. I may use it to explore the historical background of a subject, understand unfamiliar terms or identify different interpretations of a text. It gives me an initial overview, which I then develop through reading, discussion and observation.

Supporting grant writing

I sometimes use AI while preparing grant proposals, festival applications and project descriptions. It can suggest a basic structure or help arrange the information more clearly. Once I have that framework, I rewrite the content to reflect the project accurately and make the language sound like our own.

Creating promotional content

AI is also useful when we are developing social media posts, captions or promotional material for a production. Since theatre groups regularly need to communicate about rehearsals, performances and events, having an initial draft saves time. I then edit it according to the tone and identity of the production.

Refining communication

At times, I use AI to simplify a paragraph, shorten a message or present the same information in a more accessible way. This is useful when communicating with different audiences, including performers, collaborators, festival organisers and the public.

A practical collaborator

For me, AI works best as a supporting tool. It helps me begin research, organise information, develop basic structures and handle repetitive writing tasks more quickly. This gives me more time to focus on rehearsals, performers, storytelling and the creative decisions that shape the final production.

articles.title: The fear of being ‘cringe’
articles.summary:
There was a time when embarrassment faded with the moment. You tripped, people laughed, and life moved on.

Today, embarrassment can feel permanent. A single video, comment, or expression can be replayed, shared, and judged long after the moment has passed. Somewhere along the way, ‘cringe’ stopped being internet slang and became something else: a reason not to try.

Aastha Lakhey, psychologist, mental health practitioner, trainer, and lecturer, explains how the fear of being labelled ‘cringe’ reflects our need for acceptance, how social media has amplified self-consciousness, and why constantly performing for others can distance us from ourselves.

The word ‘cringe’ has become one of the strongest social judgments online. From a psychological perspective, what does the fear of being seen as cringe actually represent?

Cringe is usually used to describe something that feels awkward or too expressive in front of others. In simple terms, it has become a modern label for social discomfort.

Psychologically, the fear of being seen as cringe is really a fear of social disapproval. Humans are built for connection, and acceptance from others has always played a strong role in emotional security. When someone fears being called cringe, they are often imagining rejection in a very immediate way.

What stands out today is how quickly this judgment travels online. A small expression can feel like it is being evaluated by many people at once. So even simple self-expression starts feeling risky.

At the core, it is less about the word itself and more about a basic question people carry: “Am I still acceptable if I show who I really am?”

Why has the fear of embarrassment become so powerful today?

Embarrassment is not new. It is a normal social emotion that helps people understand boundaries in social life. What has changed is the scale and visibility of it.

In earlier settings, embarrassment usually stayed within a small group and faded quickly. Today, social media can make a moment feel permanent and widely seen. That changes how people anticipate mistakes.

Psychologically, we also tend to overestimate how much others notice us. Many studies on what is called the ‘spotlight effect’ show that people believe others are paying far more attention to their actions than they actually are.

When this belief combines with constant visibility, even small risks start feeling larger than they are. Over time, avoidance feels safer than expression.

How has social media changed self-consciousness? Do people see themselves through an imagined audience?

Yes, this is something we see quite often now.

Many people are no longer just experiencing moments. They are also imagining how those moments would appear to others. It becomes a kind of parallel awareness running in the background.

Psychologically, this relates to self-awareness and impression management. We naturally think about how we are seen by others, but social media strengthens this habit by making feedback visible and immediate.

With time, this can shift into everyday life. People may pause before speaking, dressing, or reacting, almost as if an audience is present even when it is not.

Why are humans so sensitive to other people's opinions?

This sensitivity is deeply ancestral. We are social beings, and belonging has always been tied to emotional safety.

From an evolutionary point of view, being accepted by a group once meant protection and survival. Even today, the emotional system still responds strongly to approval and rejection.

Some psychological models also suggest that self-esteem works like a signal of how accepted we feel. So when people feel judged, it does not just feel like feedback. It feels personal.

The challenge begins when external opinions start shaping how a person values themselves internally.

What happens when someone suppresses parts of themselves to avoid judgment?

At first, it often looks like adjustment or caution. Over time, it can become a pattern of hiding parts of the self.

Psychologists like Carl Rogers spoke about the idea of congruence, where a person's inner experience and outer expression stay aligned. When there is a gap between the two, people often begin to feel disconnected from themselves.

Over time, people become emotionally distant from their own identity. People may function well socially, yet feel unsure of what they actually like or feel. It can also affect self-esteem, since acceptance is then based on performance rather than authenticity.

Can constant self-curation change identity?

Yes. When decisions are repeatedly guided by how others might respond, attention slowly shifts away from personal preference. People begin to evaluate choices externally before internally.

From a psychological perspective, autonomy is important for well-being. When autonomy reduces, identity can start feeling unclear or borrowed.

Many people only notice this when they ask themselves simple questions like what they actually enjoy, without thinking about how it looks to others.

Is fear of cringe replacing fear of failure or rejection?

I would not say it is replacing older fears. It feels more like a modern form of them.

Cringe is often experienced as a kind of social rejection, especially among younger people. It carries a sense of being laughed at or dismissed.

What has changed is the visibility of that judgment. Even the possibility of being seen as awkward can stop people from trying.

But psychologically, growth still works the same way. People build confidence through experience, not avoidance.

What happens when people avoid vulnerability for too long?

Avoiding vulnerability can feel protective in the short term. It reduces discomfort and risk.

Over time, it also reduces opportunity. People stop having experiences that test their confidence or expand their sense of self.

Relationships are especially affected. Real closeness depends on being seen in an honest way. Without that, connections often remain surface-level.

Gradually, people may feel more isolated, even when they are socially active.

What would you say to someone afraid of being judged or called cringe?

I would say that the fear makes sense, but it should not take over a person's life.

Every meaningful experience carries some level of discomfort. Trying something new, expressing yourself, or showing emotion always involves uncertainty.

Most people are far more focused on themselves than on judging others. This is something psychology consistently shows.

If life becomes too focused on avoiding embarrassment, it also becomes smaller. And often, the moments people later value most are the ones where they allowed themselves to be seen, even imperfectly.

articles.title: For Kathmandu’s youths, running is about more than fitness
articles.summary:
Over the years, many youths from Kathmandu are joining running clubs as a part of their regular fitness routines. With Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and Strava popularising the trend, individuals gather mostly to enhance fitness and community, occasionally aligned with charity purposes.

As this active outdoor culture is fostering a community of health conscious individuals, questions remain regarding those it can cater to with its monetary membership requirements.

Kabita Kharel, the founder of Revive Fitness and the owner of Revive Supplements discusses the rise of running clubs in Kathmandu, popular routes, mental health benefits and the membership process.

Why are young people turning to running specifically, over gyms or other sports?

It is happening for several reasons rather than just a growing interest in fitness.

Many young adults work or study long hours and spend much of their time online. Running clubs offer a chance to meet people with similar interests, make friends, and build a routine. For many, the social aspect is as important as the exercise. Unlike other sports, running requires relatively little equipment—a good pair of shoes and comfortable clothing. This makes it accessible to students and young professionals.

Awareness of mental health, cardiovascular fitness, and healthy lifestyles has increased especially after COVID 19. People are more aware about health and fitness all around the world including Nepal. Running is seen as an effective way to reduce stress, improve mood, and stay fit without needing a gym membership.

Instagram, Strava, and TikTok have made running more visible. Sharing race medals, sunrise runs, personal bests, and group photos has encouraged others to join. Kathmandu now hosts more road races, charity runs, and trail-running events than it did a decade ago. These events give runners goals to train for and create excitement around the sport.

Most clubs meet early in the morning or on weekends, making it easy for office workers, entrepreneurs, and students to participate before starting their day. Many members say they initially joined to improve fitness but stayed because running helped them manage stress, anxiety, and work pressure. Group runs also reduce the isolation that some young people experience.

Kathmandu has a large population of young professionals and university students, growing fitness awareness, and an active outdoor culture. Running clubs combine exercise, networking, and recreation in a city where people often seek activities that don’t require expensive memberships.

How much of this is about fitness versus social life?

The answer is both—but for many young people, the community is what keeps them coming back. Group runs create a welcoming environment where everyone—from beginners to experienced runners—can participate. Social media amplifies this sense of belonging by showcasing group photos, achievements, and shared experiences.

Over time, the community becomes the reason they stay. The friendships, encouragement, and routine make it easier to keep showing up—even on days when motivation is low.

What was the running culture here like five years ago compared to now?

Five years ago, Kathmandu’s running scene was much smaller and more niche than it is today.

Earlier, Running was mainly for marathon enthusiasts - military athletes and police training . Most people ran alone for individualism.

Now it’s for everyone including youngsters, professionals, fitness enthusiasts . Today people run in large numbers. A lot of fitness platforms approach office houses, schools and other places to inspire people to stay active, organise trail runs, charity runs, 5km races and host events to attract wider audiences .

Do you think this is a lasting shift in how young Nepalis approach fitness, or a passing trend?

I think it’s more likely a lasting shift than a passing trend. This culture for me looks sustainable because fitness has become part of people’s identity.

For many young Nepalese, fitness is no longer just about losing weight. It’s becoming part of how they spend their free time, make friends, and express themselves. Running clubs, gyms, cycling groups, and hiking communities all reflect this broader lifestyle change.

Health awareness is much higher than it was a decade ago. Young people are more informed about the benefits of exercise for physical and mental health. That awareness is unlikely to disappear.

However, not everyone who joins a running club today will still be running in five years. Some people are drawn by social media trends, Fear of missing out (FOMO), posting race photos and achievements

As with many lifestyle trends, some participants will lose interest once the novelty fades.

Some people say running clubs are more of an 'urban, well-off youth' thing. Would you agree with that, or is that not a fair picture?

I think there’s some truth to that observation.

The recent boom in organised running clubs in Nepal is indeed concentrated among urban, relatively well-off young adults, especially in Kathmandu. However, that doesn’t mean running itself belongs only to that group.

Organised running clubs tend to attract people who live in cities like Kathmandu, Lalitpur, or Pokhara, have predictable work or study schedules, can afford quality running shoes and sportswear, use apps like Strava or Instagram and enjoy the social aspect of group runs and have access to parks, running routes, and organised events.

In that sense, the stereotype has some basis. Running itself is much broader than running clubs. Many of these aren’t part of the social-media-driven running culture at all.

There is also a practical factor. While running is relatively inexpensive compared with many sports, participating in the club culture often involves additional costs such as race entry fees and sometimes coffee or breakfast after group runs.

In other words, the organised running-club movement may currently skew urban and middle class, while running as a sport and form of exercise is much more diverse. Those are two related but different phenomena.

Where do these runs normally happen and how can people participate?

Most organised runs in Kathmandu happen early in the morning (around 5:30–7:00 AM) on weekdays or weekends, when traffic and pollution are lower.

Some of the most popular locations include:

Tundikhel – One of the city’s classic running spots with a relatively flat route, popular for interval training and group meetups.

Bagmati Corridor – Increasingly popular because of its longer uninterrupted stretches, making it suitable for easy runs and tempo workouts.

Swayambhunath and nearby hills – A favorite for trail runners and those looking for hill training.

Patan/UN Park and Jhamsikhel area – Frequently used by running clubs based in Lalitpur.

Shivapuri National Park trails – A weekend destination for longer trail runs and endurance training.

The participation process is usually very easy.

Find a local running club through Instagram, Facebook, or Strava. For example, Kathmandu Running Club has an active Strava community that welcomes new members.

Check their weekly schedule. Many clubs post the meeting point, distance, pace groups, and start time a few days before each run.

Show up a little early with comfortable running shoes and water. Most beginner-friendly clubs don’t require membership for a first run.

Introduce yourself to the organizers. Running clubs are generally welcoming to newcomers and often divide runners into different pace groups so beginners don’t feel left behind.

Many clubs also organise more than just runs, they’ll have coffee meetups, workshops, charity runs, and race training programs, which is one reason they’ve become so popular

articles.title: ‘Nepali cinema needs new stories, not recycled formulas’
articles.summary:
Jiwan Jung Basnyat is an actor from Sunsari. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Film Studies (Acting) from Oscar International College and has been acting in theatres since he was 12 years old.

Basnyat changed schools multiple times by Class 6, following his elder brother, a teacher. It was during this itinerant childhood that he was first introduced to theatre, almost by accident.

In the absence of an established theatre culture in his hometown, his journey began without knowing what ‘theatre’ was, which now has spanned over 200 short films, with 50 of them released and a notable work in recent Nepali film ‘Ramita Ko Pirati’.

With The Post’s Jony Nepal, he spoke about his transition from stage to screen and what it takes for actors to find recognition in today’s Nepali film industry.

What inspired you to move into films from theatre?

Once, while watching the movie ‘Chhadke 1’, I saw Bipin Karki play a character called ‘Bindu’, a gangster from Chitwan. Watching it, I realised how seamless the acting was. I believed Karki was actually from Chitwan. It was only later I found out he was a theater actor. That's when it hit me, theater people can do films too. That connected my interest in film with my continuity in theater.

With this, back when I was in grade 8, I messaged the director of ‘Bhutan’, also the principal of Oscar College.

What do you think Nepali audiences and producers should understand about the effort actors put into acting?

Audiences see and feel what's real, so there's not much for them to understand differently. But producers should focus on proper, wise casting, using a real casting process with auditions and screen tests to see if someone genuinely suits a role, instead of casting based on social media followers and personal networking.

It's frustrating watching someone get a lead role after just a random lip-sync trend clip on TikTok, while others with years of proper training and stage experience don't get a chance.

How important is self-promotion for actors?

Extremely important. This is the age of algorithms and reels. The real issue is that trained actors are being forced into promoting themselves through reels just to be seen at all.

Projects I did two or three years ago were just sitting unused on my drive; once I posted them as reels, offers from films actually started coming in.

Personally, when things were financially tough with no work, no money to pay off debt, not even enough to eat, that's when I posted my first clip. It came from real pain, not from ‘selling sympathy’ as few people called it. That said, there is a negative side to this too, many people post reels purely to chase followers, and some without any acting background end up getting mainstream recognition just for that.

What role do costumes and makeup play in developing the emotional layers for a character?

Makeup plays a big role, but only when used properly. Earlier, I used to focus a lot on the outer look with costume and makeup. But now I understand that it is secondary. The first thing is the character's psychology, their mental state, and what situation they're going through. The same thing can be perceived completely differently by different characters; that emotional layer and inner acting is what I now prioritise, more than outer appearance.

Having said that, to help myself believe in my character’s existence within me, I use music, costume, or even my co-actor's reactions become valuable.

What is your opinion on acting education and training in Nepal?

Film colleges brought technical improvement in cinematography and sound. But lately it has degraded. Short-term acting classes run for a month or two without any proper syllabus, and nobody really knows who's teaching or how qualified they are.

Even Bachelor's programs, which should teach specialisation over four years, struggle to do this properly. They fail to develop real industry connections. In my batch, there were 25-30 acting students, and only one or two are getting to work.

Colleges take fees, teach loosely, and do not help students get connected to the industry afterward.

Why do Nepali films struggle to get recognition?

The main reason is a lack of diversity; everyone copies whatever formula last worked. If ‘Loot’ works, everyone else will make ‘Loot’. Such is the case with ‘Purna Bahadur Ko Sarangi’ and many other Nepali films and trends. There's also a shortage of skilled writers and directors in the mainstream.

Real change needs producers and directors who understand cinema and are willing to trust emerging actors and filmmakers.

It is not that we do not have creative artists with expertise and unconventional vision. As the gap between the producers and us persists, so do quality products in Nepali film industry.

I personally made a portfolio of short films and pitched scripts to directors and producers, but most producers only care about finance, not filmmaking knowledge. They kept saying ‘only Purna Bahadur type films will run’, discouraging new stories. With Nepali films increasingly honing the technicalities, be it cinematography, colour grading or art direction, the lack of narrative uniqueness limits their own creative boundaries and audience.

Where do you see the Nepali film industry in the next 10 years?

There are a lot of possibilities. Talented new writers and directors are emerging, if even one of them breaks through the mainstream recognition, it opens doors for other talents too. If new, creative ideas keep coming, I believe Nepali audiences will embrace new tastes as well.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.
